#4614. Art, philosophy, and science blend in beautiful wildlife photography

Published Nov 7, 2026 5:01 PM EST

Excerpted from UNITED NATURE by Andrew Zuckerman. Copyright © 2026 by Andrew Zuckerman. Published in the United States by Crown, an imprint of the Crown Publishing Group, a division of Penguin Random House LLC.

For as long as I can remember, I have made images. Much of my childhood was spent in the darkroom in my parents’ basement, surrounded by the smell of chemicals and the magic of forms slowly appearing on paper. Of all the things I’ve pursued in my life, the camera has been the one constant. It has shaped how I see: a device that slows me down, compels me to look more deeply and to understand the subjects on an essential level. And for me, the subject has always been other forms of life.

In that sense, I am part of a long tradition. The very first images humans made were not of themselves, but of other beings. Almost forty thousand years ago, in the caves of Chauvet in France, someone painted lions, rhinoceroses, mammoths, and bears with striking naturalism, allowing the animals to emerge from the contours and relief of the stone walls. Nearly twenty thousand years later, in the caves of Lascaux, we find more painted walls: herds of horses in motion and bison colliding, painted with sophisticated perspective and composition. Humans have never stopped depicting other beings. In Egypt, cats and jackals accompanied the dead into eternity. Dolphins appear again and again on Greek pottery. In medieval manuscripts, we find lions and owls used to represent human virtues and vices. Enlightenment engravers focused on the natural world, seeking order through detail. A generation later, John James Audubon’s The Birds of America presented perhaps the most realistic natural history illustration: life-size depictions of herons, warblers, and owls, rendered with exquisite precision.

With the arrival of photography two centuries ago, the human act of depicting the natural world shifted profoundly. This was not just a new tool, it was a rupture: the first time nature could enact itself with a fidelity and presence previously unseen. The world’s first published book of photographs arrived in 1843: Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions by Anna Atkins. Atkins treated paper with a chemical solution, added specimens onto the treated paper, and left them under sunlight. This produced a white silhouette against a blue background. Atkins created these pictures of algae at the height of botanical illustration. While her peers were exhibiting artistic mastery over nature, she was removing herself. Here, the algae left its own impression directly on the paper. The plant depicted itself. The plant had agency.

One year after Atkins’s algae cyanotypes, William Henry Fox Talbot published The Pencil of Nature, a book containing twenty-four calotypes, the first paper negative, which allowed multiple positive prints to be made from a single negative. Photography was so new that Talbot felt required to include a notice: “The plates of the present work are impressed by the agency of Light alone, without any aid whatsoever from the artist’s pencil. They are the sun-pictures themselves, and not, as some persons have imagined, engravings in imitation.” Like Atkins, Talbot emphasized that the image was not mediated by the hand of the artist but drawn directly by nature itself—“sun-pictures” made by light. These early inventors of photography were introducing a new way of observing and recording the living world—one in which nature was no longer simply depicted, but allowed to speak for itself.

Only a few years later, in 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, advancing the radical idea that all life was in flux and that variation, adaptation, and transformation were the fundamental conditions of existence. In this light, Atkins’s cyanotypes seem almost prophetic: life depicted not as a fixed emblem to be mastered, but as a living process.

Skipping forward to the late nineteenth century, Cherry Kearton was pioneering what is now considered wildlife photography by hiding in hollowed-out ox carcasses or building bird-shaped blinds to get close to subjects. In the early twentieth century, photography extended into motion. Eadweard Muybridge’s studies of horses and birds revealed the invisible mechanics of gait and flight, moments too fast for the human eye to clock. Jacques Cousteau created ocean documentaries that gave the general population access to and intimacy with distant species.

By the late twentieth century, nature photography and film had become not only a way of seeing, but also a way of caring—shaping public consciousness about endangered species, vanishing habitats, and the fragility of ecosystems.

This notion of the image as a tool to influence our thinking found perhaps its most profound expression in the late 1960s, when Stewart Brand lobbied NASA to release the first photographs of the whole Earth seen from space. When those images finally appeared on the cover of his Whole Earth Catalog, they offered a new planetary perspective: not a map or an illustration, but the living sphere itself. For the first time, humanity could see Earth as a singular organism.

That one image—blue oceans swirling with white clouds, landmasses without borders—reshaped the cultural imagination. It gave rise to the environmental movement, inspired new sciences of systems and ecology, and embedded the idea that the planet itself is alive into the culture.

In the decades that followed, technology expanded the reach of our seeing. Satellite imagery made the whole Earth continuously observable: forests shrinking, glaciers collapsing, storms forming in real time. Microscopy revealed networks of neurons firing, cells dividing, viruses mutating. Telescopes peered to the edges of the universe, returning images of galaxies colliding and stars being born. Today, cameras can show bacteria and galaxies with equal fidelity.

Each age has found its own surface, its own technique, but the effort has always been an attempt at understanding both the lives of others and our own experience. Across this long arc, from the walls of Chauvet to the cyanotypes of Atkins, from Muybridge’s horses to Brand’s Whole Earth, images of the living world have not only recorded what is here, but affected how we think and feel about it. They remind us that seeing is never neutral: It is always an act of framing, and an invitation to imagine our place within the larger weave of existence.

The frame itself is an extraordinary tool of delineation. As an editor, it decides what belongs and what does not. The power of the frame lies in its capacity to determine which information matters.

My focus then started to come out in how I made pictures. The subject itself mattered less to me than resolving how to present it. Eventually, I found the pure white background, where the image becomes an encounter: a relation between two living beings shaped by a shared evolutionary history.

The white background was never an aesthetic choice. It’s purely functional. We never look at something singularly, but rather are simultaneously looking at the subject in relation to ourselves. I’ve often felt that our sense of ourselves is not a figure, it’s an abstraction. We don’t think of ourselves as a figure in relation to the ground. And so when wanting to provide the opportunity of connection to the subject—the other—that subject presented on white creates a shared plane for it and us. White space isn’t empty. It’s a condition that allows perception to happen. It lets the image reach the body before it’s interpreted by the mind. In that space, assumptions can fall away and the subject can be encountered in a preconceptual field, before meaning has settled.

Artist and creative director Andrew Zuckerman has spent 30 years traveling the world capturing the alluring and spectacular world of nature. Known for creating hyper-real images set against stark backgrounds, his artworks have been exhibited and acquired by public institutions and private collections throughout the world, and his books have been published in several international editions. Alongside his artistic practice, he has advised and led creative work for pioneering companies in technology, climate innovation, and energy, including Apple and Google. He lives in New York City with his wife and three children.

#4611. Honda’s HRC Performance Parts Business Was a Long Time Coming

Oh, and the Civic Type R HRC concept? Yeah, it’s gonna be sold here in the United States.

Honda has made no secret of its plans to eventually enter the performance parts business with HRC-branded components. This is part of a larger campaign to turn the HRC brand—now the global name for all Honda motorsports activities—into a performance footprint on par with Nissan’s Nismo or BMW’s M. And like those brands, it sure seems like complete production models will be sold with that performance badge, too.

Both HRC performance parts and HRC road cars were a hot topic at the 2026 SEMA Show, where the company showed off race cars, custom builds, and one very interesting concept. In an interview with Road & Track, HRC U.S. senior vice president Jon Ikeda made it clear that the Civic Type R HRC concept on display (seen below) was “going to be sold here.”

“We’ve shared with everyone that it’s coming here,” Ikeda added, “and we’re really excited about it. We have big debuts coming next year—at the Tokyo Auto Salon, a big debut there. We’re just happy that our region is included; there are a lot of people who are excited about it here.”

While he stopped short of confirming similar plans for an Acura Integra Type S HRC, Ikeda noted that consumer interest is strong and suggested that the company “[has] to seriously think about doing it.”

An HRC Integra may not be a lock, but Honda has already confirmed that the four-door Acura will join the Civic Type R in receiving performance parts offered directly by HRC. Ikeda notes that the Integra’s offerings will include wheels from 2Elle, the supplier of the forged wheels used on the recently-retired ARX-06 race car. Those, and other components, were tested on an Integra Type S at the Nürburgring Nordschleife ahead of the SEMA showcase. Ikeda mentions the value of these parts being sold directly by the OEM—a major distinction that keeps options open for owners worried about voiding a warranty or decreasing a car’s resale value.

“As soon as you accessorize,” he continues, “you void your warranty on things. If you own a Honda car, you do a third party purchase of a spring or something, you devalue your vehicle. By creating OEM parts, you’re able to honor the warranty when you buy the car, you can even finance it, bundle it up in your financing if you want if you do it at the dealership. If you have all the OEM parts to upgrade, it’s not a new business framework. Others are doing it. We have a very equitable brand to say, ‘hey, you’ve got OEM HRC parts, put it on your car, get your warranty, don’t devalue your vehicle, enjoy the ride.’ That’s a big, big part of it.”

HRC parts will begin arriving at dealers in the first quarter of next year. The HRC-badged Civic Type R should be revealed at the Tokyo Auto Salon in January.

#4610. How do porta potties work?

Published Nov 8, 2026 8:03 AM EST

We’ve all used them. Whether at festivals, campgrounds, construction sites, or even weddings, porta potties are an unavoidable—and often underappreciated—part of modern life. They’re the unsung heroes of moments when bathrooms are few and far between, faithfully answering nature’s call, one flushless visit at a time.

But how do porta potties work, exactly? They’re so commonplace—and so universally dreaded—that most people try to get in, do their business, and get out as quickly as possible, without giving much thought to what’s happening. But plug your nose, lift the lid, and brave a peek inside, and you’ll find a simple yet elegant system designed to reliably meet one of humanity’s most basic needs.

Conventional toilets rely on a combination of water, pressure, and gravity to do their job. When you flush, water rushes from the tank into the bowl, pushing waste down through a curved pipe called a trap and into the plumbing system.

From there, the wastewater travels through sewer pipes to a treatment plant or, in some instances, a septic system. A small amount of water remains behind in the trap, creating a seal that prevents sewer gases from wafting back into the bathroom.

Once the process is complete, the tank refills with clean water from the plumbing system, typically from a municipal water supply or private well, and the porcelain throne is ready for its next user.

Portable toilets—also known as portaloos, portajohns, and a variety of other nicknames—use water, too. But that’s about where the similarities end. “There’s no plumbing, and it really doesn’t smell good,” says Walt Terry, director of operations for Metro Services, a family-owned portable toilet and dumpster rental company in Little Rock, Arkansas. “It’s not the most pleasant thing in the world.”

Modern porta potties come in a variety of shapes and sizes, from swanky multi-stall trailers to no-frills cubicles. The standard plastic model you see at events has a relatively simple design, one that traces its roots to George Hardig. Hardig filed a late-1960s patent for porta potties. Later he became a co-founder of PolyJohn Enterprises, still one of the leading portable toilet manufacturers today.

Made of large, rigid plastic panels, Hardig’s invention was designed to be weather- and insect-proof, simple to clean and maintain, and lightweight and easy to move. His model was cylindrical and featured a removable toilet tank, while today’s are usually rectangular and have the holding tank built-in. But other than that, not much has changed in porta potty design since Hardig first developed his portable toilet “cabana” nearly six decades ago.

These tall boxes have a large empty cavity at the back, topped by a toilet seat. When users do their business, waste simply drops down into the large, roomy hole beneath.

“It’s just a big void space,” says Katie Gossett, office manager for Tidy Tim’s, Inc., a portable restroom and septic service company her dad started more than 30 years ago in central Ohio.

“The holding tanks can vary a bit in size, but your average is like 25 to 30 gallons.”

The holding tank is filled with some amount of water, typically between five and 10 gallons, as well as a special, dark-blue chemical cocktail that serves numerous purposes. It helps keep the funky odors under control and starts to break down the waste and toilet paper, while also hiding the tank’s contents. The color is also a key indicator of a porta potty’s freshness.

“It will actually turn green once it’s not working anymore—when it gets there, it’s not a good sight,” says Terry. “The chemical goes in there and does as much as it can, until it can’t.”

There’s another easily overlooked component that helps keep porta potties from getting too stinky: the vent pipe. The next time you use a portable toilet, look up at the roof. You’ll spot a small pipe protruding from the back corner, discreetly drawing foul gases out of the holding tank and venting them into the air.

Some models also have built-in urinals, which simply funnel urine into the holding tank for those who prefer to remain standing when they pee.

When it’s time to service a porta potty, specially trained employees from the rental company arrive with a powerful vacuum truck. They use a hose to suck out the tank’s liquids and solids, transferring the waste into the truck for disposal.

Many vacuum trucks also have a separate compartment filled with clean water, which staffers then use to wash out the porta potty’s entire interior—the tank, as well as the walls, ceiling, and floors.

Sanitizing spray and a quick wipedown with a microfiber towel finishes the job—which is a lot less gross than you might imagine. “Our guys know what they’re doing,” says Gossett. “I’m not going to say accidents don’t happen, but most of the time, when they get [back to the office], they are exactly the way they left. They very rarely get dirty.”

Airplane seats really are getting smaller

Rental companies typically service their units on a regular schedule, going around to the various porta potties they own and sucking out all the waste. Once the vacuum truck is full, they drive to a local wastewater treatment facility and dump it.

“It’s like a city sewer plant that is able to add some to their load,” says Gossett. “Their treatment plant is big enough that they can take on that extra waste and process it for us.”

The servicing schedule varies, but a good rule of thumb is that one portable restroom can accommodate 10 people during a typical 40-hour workweek before it needs to be cleaned out.

And, no, unless something wild happens, your porta potty probably isn’t going to overflow.

“A lot of people worry that they’re going to fill up, but usually that’s not the case,” says Kade Jensen, the owner of Minty Pine Sanitation Solutions Ltd. in southern Alberta, Canada.

Porta potties have gotten a bad rap over the years. Yet there’s an entire corner of the internet that’s apparently fascinated by what happens when they get cleaned out.

A post shared by Minty Pine Cleans (@mintypinecleans)

Jensen, who is 23, found that out a few months ago, when he started posting regular point-of-view videos of his porta potty cleanouts on social media. Each one starts with a direct look into the full tank, but ends with the oddly satisfying payoff of a squeaky-clean unit.

Since then, he’s watched his company’s follower count skyrocket, and his views climb into the hundreds of millions. “A lot of people have always seen [porta potties] and used them, but they don’t know the exact process,” he says.

“It’s almost like people want to look away but they can’t look away at the same time. It’s something you’re not used to seeing.”

When he first started posting videos, Jensen says, he was simply having fun. But the response has given him a new perspective: He now sees the videos as a way to pull back the curtain on an industry that most people would rather not think about—and show that portable restrooms aren’t nearly as revolting as their reputation suggests.

“Our whole thing is that it really doesn’t have to be gross,” he says. “It’s really not as scary or gross as people make it out to be.”

#4607. Subcompact SUVs May Seem Appealing, but Compact Cars Are Often a Better Buy

Unless you’re dead set on the tall seating position that an SUV provides, we think these small hatchbacks are far more satisfying than their crossover siblings.

Sure, SUVs are popular, but that doesn’t mean they’re always the best choice for your needs. The smaller an SUV gets, the fewer advantages it offers when compared with an equivalent sedan or hatchback. Here, we’re looking at the subcompact SUV segment and stacking up these small crossovers against compact cars from the same brand.

Subcompact SUVs are the smallest of their species. As the name suggests, they’re smaller than compact SUVs, and their tidier footprints often mean compromises in space, fuel economy, and driving satisfaction.

Automakers feel the need to offer additional ground clearance and all-wheel drive in these SUV models to justify their categorization. But these models typically share the same underpinnings and engines as their compact-car kin.

This means these SUV models are often heavier, less enjoyable to drive, and less fuel-efficient than their non-SUV siblings. Both types of vehicles also typically offer similar amounts of cargo and passenger space. Pricing, meanwhile, tends to favor the compact hatchbacks.

If these two types of vehicles are so similar, then why the different classifications? Blame size creep.

Cars and SUVs typically get larger with each passing generation. Let’s roll the clock back 25 years. While most modern compact cars are bigger than their counterparts from a quarter century ago, they still tend to cast smaller shadows than mid-size cars from the turn of the millennium.

On the other hand, the subcompact SUVs of today are typically larger than the compact SUVs of 25 years ago. Due to this, calling a modern SUV “subcompact” better describes its size relative to the overall SUV landscape as opposed to the larger passenger-vehicle space.

Odds are that if you’re shopping for one of these small-sized SUVs, you’re going to be just as well—if not better—served by these vehicles’ often less expensive and more fun-to-drive compact hatchback stablemates.

The HR-V is Honda's smallest SUV, but it’s still plenty spacious inside. The main downside of this model is that it’s available with only one powertrain: a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter inline-four that produces just 158 horsepower.

This means the HR-V accelerates at a leisurely pace. In our testing, this little Honda SUV needed 9.4 seconds to hit 60 mph.

The HR-V earns an EPA-estimated combined rating of 28 mpg in front-drive form. Adding all-wheel drive drops that figure to 27 mpg.

The Honda Civic hatchback has the same base engine as the CR-V, but it also offers a more powerful and more fuel-efficient hybrid variant that has quicker acceleration and much better fuel economy—up to 49 mpg combined, according to the EPA. The Civic doesn’t offer all-wheel drive as the HR-V does, but we’d advocate for a good set of winter tires instead.

In our testing, the Civic hatchback’s cargo area was only marginally smaller than the HR-V’s. It held six carry-on suitcases behind the rear seat, which is only one fewer case than the HR-V can accommodate.

More importantly, the Civic is far more fun to drive than the HR-V.

The Subaru Crosstrek is the spiritual successor to the old Impreza Outback Sport, which was essentially an Impreza hatchback with added body cladding. Compared to the old Outback Sport, the Crosstrek is a bit more distinct than the Impreza it’s based on. Even so, the Crosstrek is still effectively a lifted Impreza hatch with additional ground clearance and more rugged looks. As such, we don’t think the Crosstrek is worth the extra cost over the run-of-the-mill Impreza hatchback that Subaru still offers.

Subaru makes an even better case for the Impreza hatch for 2027 courtesy of a new base model that starts at less than $26,000. As we previously detailed, the Impreza beats the Crosstrek in nearly every metric in our testing: It’s quicker, more fuel-efficient, and offers as much space inside. The only reason we can think of to choose the Crosstrek is for its available gas-electric hybrid powertrain or its extra ground clearance.

A redesign for 2027 brings eye-catching new looks to the Kia Seltos subcompact SUV. A 147-hp four-cylinder comes standard, while a 190-hp turbo four is optional. For its second generation, the Seltos also offers an available gas-electric hybrid powertrain—an option the Kia K4 compact hatch lacks.

Sure, the Kia K4 hatchback doesn’t offer hybrid power. However, what this handsome hatch lacks in powertrain options, it makes up for in other ways.

Simply put, we prefer the way the K4 drives to the Seltos. Credit the compact hatchback’s lower center of gravity, which improves handling and behind-the-wheel engagement.

The K4 is also more miserly than the equivalent gas-only Seltos. When fitted with the available 190-hp turbocharged 1.6-liter four-cylinder, the K4 hatch is also notably quicker than its equally powerful Seltos kin. In our testing, a so-equipped K4 hatch accelerated to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, while a turbocharged Seltos needed 8.2 seconds to hit the same mark.

We haven’t yet measured how many carry-on suitcases fit in the cargo bay of the new Seltos. Compared to the previous-generation Seltos, though, the K4 hatch fell one carry-on suitcase short of its subcompact SUV sibling’s sum.

The Mazda CX-30 is among our favorite subcompact crossover SUVs. It drives great, features a high-quality interior, and provides sufficient oomph with the standard 186-hp 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine. Opt for the 250-hp turbocharged 2.5-liter, and the all-wheel-drive CX-30 accelerates with even more vigor. But what if Mazda also sold a vehicle that paired all the positive traits of the CX-30 with a lower starting price, even better driving dynamics, and an available manual gearbox? Well, good news: It does.

The Mazda 3 hatchback may do without the higher seating position of the CX-30, but it makes up for it with livelier dynamics courtesy of its lower center of gravity and lighter curb weight. At a manufacturer-estimated 3111 pounds, the front-drive 3 hatch’s mass undercuts that of the all-wheel-drive CX-30 by 284 pounds.

While we think the available six-speed manual gearbox of the front-drive 3 makes it superior to its all-wheel-drive kin, we know not everyone will agree with us. No worries, though, because Mazda also offers the 3 with all-wheel drive. Opting for it adds 172 pounds to the curb weight of 3 hatchbacks with the standard 186-hp four. However, AWD is standard on turbocharged models.

In our testing, both the 3 hatchback and CX-30 were able to hold up to 16 carry-on suitcases with the rear seats folded. With the rear seats in place, the 3 hatch’s cargo area held five carry-on suitcases—just one fewer than the CX-30.

Acura’s subcompact SUV is about as interesting and exciting as watching C-SPAN. Short of its available all-wheel-drive system and slightly bigger interior compartment, there are few other reasons to pick the ADX over its compact hatchback sibling, the Integra.

With a starting price of $34,795, the Acura Integra undercuts the ADX by a significant $1755. It’s also significantly more enjoyable to drive and a good deal quicker.

Though both the Integra and ADX come standard with a turbocharged 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine that mates to a continuously variable automatic transmission (CVT), the Integra benefits from an extra 10 horsepower and 13 pound-feet of torque relative to the unit in the ADX. With 200 horsepower and 192 pound-feet of torque, a CVT-equipped Integra accelerated to 60 mph in a reasonable 7.1 seconds. An all-wheel-drive ADX, meanwhile, required a languid 8.7 ticks to hit 60 mph.

Admittedly, the fastback shape of the Integra cuts into its cargo-carrying capabilities. We fit 18 carry-on suitcases in its cargo bay with the rear seats folded and five with the seatbacks up. The squarer shape of the ADX afforded totals of 22 and seven, respectively.

Despite being raised on a steady diet of base-model Hondas and Toyotas—or perhaps because of it—Joey Capparella cultivated an obsession for the automotive industry throughout his childhood in Nashville, Tennessee. He found a way to write about cars for the school newspaper during his college years at Rice University, which eventually led him to move to Ann Arbor, Michigan, for his first professional auto-writing gig at Automobile Magazine. He has been part of the Hearst Autos team since 2016 and now lives in New York City.

Despite their shared last name, Greg Fink is not related to Ed "Big Daddy" Roth's infamous Rat Fink. Both Finks, however, are known for their love of cars, car culture, and—strangely—monogrammed one-piece bathing suits. Greg's career in the media industry goes back more than a decade. His previous experience includes stints as an editor at publications such as U.S. News & World Report, The Huffington Post, Motor1.com, and MotorTrend.

#4606. Polar bears are gathering close to this Canadian town—and co-existing with humans

Published Nov 8, 2026 10:17 AM EST

Polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are typically solitary creatures. But in a Canadian town on Hudson Bay, the predators gather along the coast every fall to wait for the ice to freeze.

“It’s an incredible phenomenon to experience,” Alysa McCall, director of science at Polar Bears International (PBI), tells Popular Science. “The bears return to this stretch of coast because it’s where the Bay freezes first, thanks to freshwater from the Churchill River plus the Bay’s currents and winds.”

Sea ice platforms help polar bears catch seals, which are their main source of prey. It’s usually harder for them to do so without the ice, as exemplified in a video PBI captured of a bear on the shore unsuccessfully trying to hunt a seal in the water.

This makes polar bears particularly vulnerable to climate change, which is bringing about longer ice-free seasons. In fact, polar bears in the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation today are stuck on land for around one month longer than their grandparents. What’s more, their numbers have approximately halved since 1979 because of sea ice loss.

Nicknamed the Polar Bear Capital of the World, the residents of Churchill, Manitoba have front-row seats to the annual polar bear gathering (you can also watch through their Polar Bear Live Cams). They are thus also exposed to conflict with these very large temporary neighbors, and climate change is extending this potentially dangerous overlap.

“When polar bears are on land, they are generally fasting. They sometimes venture into towns and communities to look for food, and human areas are full of things that attract curious bears – from trash bins to food smells,” McCall explains. “As climate change causes polar bears to spend more time on land, they have more opportunities to encounter people.”

As such, McCall and her colleagues at PBI have developed new tools to facilitate human-polar bear coexistence. One of them—cheekily named Bear-dar—is a medium-range polar bear detection radar currently being used at the Eureka Weather Station in Nunavut, Canada. Now the team is testing Bear-vision, a smart polar bear detection camera, at Churchill’s waste facility. According to McCall, it’s cheaper and simpler to use than Bear-dar, and works like a doorbell camera that warns you if there’s a polar bear hanging out outside.

“The team hopes to make the technology open-source so that Bear-vision will be widely available and accessible. More bear-safe tools mean fewer negative encounters, ultimately keeping people and polar bears separate and safer,” says McCall. “What’s happening along Hudson Bay shows how much communities can do to live harmoniously with nature.”

#4604. Tested: 2027 Mercedes-AMG GT 55 4-Door Proves EVs Can Be Engaging

This is an electric car that makes V-8 noises, goes like stink, and is loaded to the gills with Mercedes luxury.

Making a performance EV compelling enough to convince enthusiasts to jump on board has proven difficult, but that’s precisely what Mercedes-AMG is trying to do with the 2027 4-Door Coupe. Mercedes is going down the same path as other manufacturers and their acclaimed electric performance machines—such as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N and Genesis GV60 Magma—by simulating the experience of a car equipped with an internal-combustion engine. It’s great fun, but the efforts would be for naught if the rest of the car didn’t live up to the experience. Thankfully, this electric AMG is a ripper from every angle. Except when viewed from the rear. Maybe avoid doing that.

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

It’s hardly lesser, but the “55” in the AMG GT 55 4-Door Coupe is empirically less mighty than the “63” in the GT 63. This EV features a tri-motor powertrain made up of three axial-flux motors engineered with YASA that combine for 805 hp and 1372 pound-feet of torque. That 805 hp figure is the peak, the lesser “continuous” rating coming in at 557 hp. But if you want all the power, all the time, that can be accomplished by putting the car in Race mode, or pulling both steering-wheel paddles to activate Boost mode, which lasts for 55 seconds. Mercedes claims a 2.7-second 0–60-mph time and top speed of 186 mph should you option the AMG Performance package.

Powertrain layout: 2 rear electric motors, 1 front

Slipping behind the wheel, the first thing that struck me about the GT 55 was the properly low seating position. Excellent work there, Mercedes. After fumbling about with the confusing start/stop button on the stalk (the car doesn’t really turn on until you flick it into Drive or Reverse), I started comfortably trundling along.

The AMG Active Ride Control air suspension did a standup job on the track in the GT 63, but it’s even more remarkable on the road in the 55. An air suspension with adaptive dampers is standard, but this optional hydraulically interconnected damper system is assuredly the one you want. Combined with the multilink suspension in the front and rear, an abundance of forged aluminum components on the front axle, and rear-axle steering up to six degrees, this chassis just oozes confidence right off the bat. There was no jittery stiffness or harshness to the ride in Comfort, and it was only moderately sharper on bumps in the punchier modes. You could spend every day behind the wheel thinking you’re in a regular Mercedes and not an AMG product.

But when I found some sweepers, the front end just begged for me to keep piling on speed thanks to how stable everything feels. At points, it was almost too confidence-inspiring, as the sophisticated chassis was writing checks the GT’s 5501-pound mass and Continental SportContact 7 summer tires struggled to cash on some of southern Spain’s steep downhill slaloms. The steering and body control say go, go, but the tires quickly say they need a break from the heat. Don’t mistake that as a braking system limitation either, because the optional carbon-ceramics hold up to mega abuse. I just wish the pedal feel wasn’t so mushy and inconsistent throughout the stroke.

Accelerating out of corners, the sensation was AMG at its best. With the ESP system in Sport mode, the rear tires surrendered grip progressively and tidily. It was so consistent and predictable that it almost felt calculated, and to a degree, it is. Mercedes let me play with the AMG Race Engineer system in the 63 model on the racetrack—that’s the three dials in the center console which let the driver customize how hairy or locked down they want the experience from a traction control and yaw agility perspective. The 55 has the exact same system, given you option it. It’s fun to toy with on the track but can just as easily change the character of the car on a fast canyon road to suit your mood.

And then there’s AMGForce Sport+, the system that simulates both a V-8 engine and a multi-clutch transmission system and that proved remarkably adept at convincing me I was piloting an internal-combustion-powered car. Mercedes mimics the soundtrack and other theatrics—engine braking, seat vibrations, and shifting—from the previous-gen AMG GT R Coupe. I found myself tapping up and down the paddles through the mountains with glee for miles on end. Yeah, it’s all fake, but the alternative is a pure electric car experience that I find gets a bit boring after a short period.

Would a proper V-8 and real transmission have been more involving and addicting to wind out? Absolutely. But even if you set aside the stagecraft, this AMG is a blast to drive. It toes the line between back-road barn burner and everyday luxury like the very best AMGs of recent history. Plus, the EV hardware backing everything up is elite.

A 106-kWh battery pack developed specifically for AMG performance cars can be charged at speeds over 600 kW, allowing you to go from 10 to 80 percent in only 11 minutes. No, 600-kW chargers don’t exist in the U.S. yet, but when they arrive, this car will be ready. The system can even switch from 800 to 400 volts by virtually “splitting” the pack in half for less compromised charging at 400-volt stations, which should help tremendously at Tesla Superchargers. Range figures aren’t out yet, but Mercedes is claiming up to 434 miles on the optimistic European WLTP test, so you can rest assured that EPA numbers will be well over 300 miles.

Mercedes has clearly done some learning from all the criticism leveled at its interiors over the past half-decade. The GT’s steering wheel has a proper scroll wheel for volume and a switch for cruise control. The door-positioned seat toggles physically move when you press them (finally), and those AMG Race Engineer controls in the center console are aptly the most satisfying knobs to turn in the whole car. The quilted leather on the doors themselves is spectacular, but don’t worry, there’s plenty to wrinkle a brow at too.

Adjusting the heated and ventilated seat controls requires multiple extremely precise stabs at the touchscreen. Trying to find your way around the unending drive mode and sound mode controls will require patience for even the most tech-savvy. And while the massive screens are of superb quality in terms of both picture and response, the sheer amount of real estate dedicated to them could easily be a turn-off. On the plus side, the dedicated tachometer that pops up in Sport+ mode is probably the best digital tach fitted to a Mercedes yet. Ironic that it arrives in an EV.

Practicality doesn’t take a back seat with this long, swoopy liftback. Despite its name, this is a four-door hatchback, and unlike the Porsche Taycan, it has enough space in the rear to seat medium-to-tall adults. It doesn’t completely suck to get in or out either. In another win for the AMG over Porsche’s sport sedan, the 14.7-cubic-foot cargo area seems positively massive. You can extend it further by putting the rear seats down, leaving an impressively large space to go road-tripping or move large items with. A carbon-fiber frunk exists for smaller items, too, and it’s here you’ll find the traditional signed AMG plaque, only this one is signed by any number of folks involved in the design or engineering of the vehicle.

If you found the Taycan a little too serious or not practical enough, the AMG GT 55 4-Door Coupe might be just the EV you’re looking for. It lands in between the Taycan 4S and GTS, but is quicker than both of those Taycan variants in a straight line. The Porsche is the more serious sports car, though practicality is firmly on Mercedes’s side. The debate between the 63 and 55 is where things get a little tricky with about a $30,000 gulf between the two—the 55 starts at $146,500, the 63 at $176,550.

Then there’s the forthcoming fully electric BMW M3 to consider, but we need to wait for pricing on that. But putting that and the GT together already feels as if it will be one of the benchmark tests of 2027.

I didn’t drive the GT 63 on the road, but it didn’t feel significantly quicker than the GT 55 in a straight line. Both have the same overengineered battery pack and tri-motor powertrain. The differences are largely in the suspension and software, like the AMG Race Engineer (again, optional on the 55) and pure luxury features like massage seats and an enormous HUD. That said, when you’re spending $145K and some change for options, what’s another $30,000 to get it all? If extra-dynamic driving isn’t in your future, perhaps a base 55 without all the go-fast goodies makes fiscal sense. But otherwise, it’s hard to imagine anyone who has sold themselves on the idea of the GT 4-Door not wanting the full 63 experience.

The active rear diffuser takes moving aero to a new level of complex and cool. Mercedes says it provides a boost to efficiency on the highway, but it also helps stability at high speeds. Watching it extend and retract on the move is quite the party trick. And thankfully, you can manually extend it to show off to your friends who are stuck with passive rear diffusers on their cars.

#4602. 9 fast fixes to help you stop doomscrolling

Published Nov 8, 2026 2:11 PM EST

Doomscrolling: To spend an inordinate amount of time swiping up and down across multiple social media and news feeds—without really getting anything of use out of it. In fact, as addictive as it is, doomscrolling often leaves us feeling worse about ourselves and the world than when we started.

You might find yourself engaging in doomscrolling right before you go to bed, first thing after waking up, standing in line on the subway platform, or even—this is how bad it’s gotten—sitting at the dinner table with the family.

It doesn’t have to be this way though. There are tools and tactics you can use to beat doomscrolling and spend less time on your phone—which means more time enjoying the world and the people around you (and catching up on your sleep). Here are nine tips that can help, across all makes and models of phone.

A grayscale interface can make your phone less distracting. On Android, open Settings and pick Digital Wellbeing > Bedtime Mode to automatically switch to grayscale at a certain time, or enable it manually via Accessibility > Color and motion > Color correction.

On an iPhone, open Settings then choose Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters to find the grayscale option. There’s no automatic evening color drain like there is on Android, but you can automate the switch by using the Shortcuts app built into iOS.

Both Android and iOS now include tools for setting limits on the time you can spend inside particular apps each day. You can of course easily choose to disable these limits whenever you like, but it might still go some way to weaning you off your doomscrolling habits.

On Android, from Settings head to Digital Wellbeing > App timers to start choosing your apps and your time limits. Over on iOS, from Settings it’s Screen Time > App & Website Activity to do the same. You could even try slowly reducing your limits over time.

You might not have noticed, but there are now a wealth of apps to help wean you off unhealthy phone habits, and make sure you keep on top of your screen time. They all gamify the process in some way, encouraging and rewarding you for not doomscrolling.

Some of our favorites include Forest (for Android and iOS), Focus Friend (for Android and iOS), and Focus Traveller (for iOS): They use growing trees, helping a bean character, and hiking up a mountain, respectively, to help you stay on task and avoid distractions.

Pause Point is a new feature available now in Android 17 on Pixel devices, and potentially rolling out more widely in the future. You can find it by opening Settings and choosing Digital Wellbeing > Pause Point, then tapping Continue to get the feature configured.

For the apps that you choose, every time you open them up, you get one of your selected pause points. They include breathing exercises, and custom photo galleries, and the idea is to take a beat and consider if you really need to open up that distracting app after all.

Sometimes the apps and options on your phone aren’t enough on their own. If that’s the case, try the Brick: It’s a $59 physical dongle that uses NFC tech, and when you tap your phone against it, it enables a custom quiet mode that blocks certain websites and apps.

The idea is that the Brick essentially bricks your phone for certain periods, so you spend less time on it. It’s not the only gadget that does this trick either—you could also check out the Autonomous Key, which can be yours for a mere $19 and works along similar lines.

Both Android and iOS let you use so-called Focus modes to cut down on distractions and reduce the temptation to doomscroll. They work like a Do Not Disturb mode with extras, and you can configure different settings for sleeping, driving, or trying to get work done.

On Android, open Settings and then head to Modes; on iOS, it’s Settings and then Focus. The features work in a similar way on both platforms, letting you edit an existing Focus mode or start your own from scratch, with exemptions for certain apps and contacts.

Certain apps come with their own features for limiting the amount of time you spend in them, so it’s worth having a look through the apps that cause you to doomscroll the most to see what options you’ve got—even if it’s just dialing down the number of notifications.

Instagram is one example. Open up the profile tab, then tap the menu button (three horizontal lines) and pick Time management. From the next screen you can set yourself a daily limit, and enable a sleep mode (when notifications are muted) for specific times.

This is just for the Samsung Galaxy owners out there, and if your phone has the latest One UI 9 software installed on it, there’s a new tool available in it called AI Network Guard. It’s designed for kids, but it works well for keeping adults (i.e. you) off distracting apps too.

It’s well hidden though: From Settings, tap Connections > Wi-Fi, then the three dots in the corner. Then, tap Intelligent Wi-Fi five times to bring up the Connectivity labs entry. Here you’ll find AI Network Guard, and can choose the apps to impose usage restrictions on.

This is a classic, because the fewer notifications you get, the less likely you are to pick up your phone. There are now a host of ways to tweak alerts on both Android and iOS, but essentially it’s about limiting how and when your apps can interrupt what you’re doing.

On Android or iOS, choose Notifications from Settings to see the options open to you. You can make alerts less distracting or disable them altogether, on an app-by-app basis, and access useful features like notification snoozing (Android) or scheduled summaries (iOS).

#4601. BYD is launching this 5-seat luxury electric SUV next week with over 1,000 km of range

BYD’s luxury brand, Denza, calls it “the king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles.” The new Denza N8 electric SUV will launch next week, offering an impressive CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles), massive digital screens, and plenty of premium extras.

After opening pre-orders for the new 5-seat luxury electric SUV last week, Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, said the results so far “have been excellent.”

According to Li, the Denza N8 is “definitely the most anticipated luxury SUV of the year.” Using BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries, the Denza N8 EV has a pure electric CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) on a single charge.

That’s just as much as the N8 plug-in hybrid (PHEV) it’s replacing, which offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

While Li confirmed last week that the new EV variant would go on sale in November, he didn’t give a specific date.

Now, it’s official. Denza announced on its Weibo page on Friday that the launch event for the Denza N8 EV will be held on November 12, 2026.

BYD is still offering a limited-time promo that includes a 5,000 RMB credit for those who place a reservation with a 2,000 RMB ($200) deposit.

The Denza N8 measures 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase. That’s slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

It’s available with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8 uses BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes three electric motors: a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, for a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Regulatory filings earlier this year revealed it will use either a 130.15 kWh or 105.79 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 1,003 km (623 miles) and 800 km (497 miles), respectively.

The Denza N8 also features BYD’s latest Flash Charging technology, letting it recharge from 10% to 80% in just five minutes. It takes just nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

#4600. TAG Heuer’s Formula 1 Smartwatch Keeps Race Weekend on Your Wrist

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

We put TAG Heuer’s Connected Calibre E5 x Formula 1 Edition to the test and found its race-weekend features as practical as they are impressive.

For Formula 1 fans, keeping track of a race weekend isn’t always straightforward, especially when you’re traveling across time zones. Between practice sessions, Sprint weekends, qualifying, and the race itself, there’s plenty to keep up with. After spending September and October traveling with my boyfriend, I found that the TAG Heuer Connected Calibre E5 x Formula 1 Edition does an excellent job of making that information accessible without having to constantly reach for our phones.

What impressed me most wasn’t the watch’s appearance, although it’s certainly eye-catching. It was how seamlessly the dedicated Formula 1 app handled race schedules. It showed session times in our local time zone, eliminating the mental math that comes with following an international racing series. While I manually added sessions to my phone’s calendar to get alerts, we had the weekend’s schedule ready on his wrist. It’s a small convenience that becomes surprisingly valuable when you’re juggling travel plans around a Grand Prix.

The watch’s F1 integration goes well beyond displaying the next race. Its dedicated app provides the complete season calendar, session schedules, results, and drivers’ and constructors’ standings. A customizable widget makes it even easier to check upcoming events. The information updates automatically, though results aren't instantaneous, so this was mostly useful when we couldn’t catch P3. Very important information if you play F1 Fantasy as well.

TAG Heuer also includes 24 circuit-specific watch faces that change throughout the season. Each displays the upcoming track layout, with a seconds indicator traveling around the circuit and a gauge tracking the race weekend's progression. It's a clever detail that makes this feel like an actual Formula 1 product rather than an ordinary smartwatch with an expensive logo.

The hardware is equally impressive. The 45-mm case uses Grade 2 titanium with a black DLC coating, complemented by a ceramic bezel, sapphire crystal, and red accents. The 1.39-inch OLED display is sharp. The watch has interchangeable straps, offering options for everyday wear. But we stuck with the classic one provided.

Underneath, Qualcomm's Snapdragon Wear 5100+ processor powers TAG Heuer's proprietary operating system. The watch supports both iOS and Android. As an Apple user, I can only speak to how it handled the iOS integration. The GPS and fitness tracking were on point during a few hours of hiking in Pennsylvania. TAG Heuer claims up to three days of battery life in low-power mode, with a full recharge taking approximately 90 minutes. These are manufacturer figures, not endurance results from our travel experience. We charged it fully twice a week, using the watch to its true potential.

My biggest complaint is the size. At 45 mm, this is a substantial watch, and I genuinely wish TAG Heuer offered a smaller edition. As a female fan, I'd happily wear one myself, but the current dimensions make it a less appealing option for smaller wrists.

Then there's the $2,550 price. You can certainly find smartwatches with comparable everyday functionality for considerably less. What you're paying for here is TAG Heuer’s craftsmanship, premium materials, and a genuinely useful, integrated Formula 1 experience.

This isn't a necessary purchase for watching F1, but it's an excellent luxury accessory for dedicated fans. After seeing how effortlessly it kept our race weekends organized while traveling, I understand its appeal. Now, TAG Heuer, please make a smaller one.

#4599. 2027 Kawasaki Jet Skis deliver a supercharged, eye-opening performance

Published Nov 8, 2026 5:21 PM EST

In 1964, then-Pontiac division president John Z. Delorean (yes, that Delorean, of Back to the Future movie car fame) invented the muscle car category by bolting the big-block V8 engine from the company’s full-size cars into its lighter intermediate-sized chassis to create the legendary Pontiac GTO.

Kawasaki has done the same thing for its Jet Skis for the 2027 model year by installing the 310-horsepower supercharged 1.5-liter engine from its bigger Ultra models into the sporty, agile Jet Ski STX hull. The result is a truly eye-opening performance with what the company says is its quickest Jet Ski yet.

Kawasaki established the personal watercraft industry with the 1973 introduction of the 27-horsepower JS400 Jet Ski. Since that time, however, the one-time industry leader has slipped in popularity compared to its rivals in the market.

The company’s 2027 plan to recapture customers includes an embrace of high performance. Kawasaki has rolled out five new models for 2027, but the stars of the show are the high-performance Jet Skis meant to excite customers.

The original Jet Ski employed a smokey 400 cc 2-stroke engine that grew to 800 cc over time. Those early Jet Skis were tricky stand-up models that delivered responsive handling but presented a learning curve that saw newcomers falling off repeatedly as they learned to master the machine.

The solution was the introduction of the more stable sit-down models that traded responsiveness for stability. It was a trade that so many riders were willing to make that eventually Kawasaki phased out the stand-up models entirely.

The industry shifted to cleaner 4-stroke engines in the ‘90s, and 1999 saw the arrival of the 1.5-liter engine based on Kawasaki’s sport motorcycle powerplants in its Jet Skis, packing 150 horsepower. In 2007, the engineering team bolted a supercharger to the same engine, producing 250 horsepower.

Now, thanks to the technology of Eaton’s Twin Vortices System supercharger design (which debuted on the 2009 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1), power has reached 310 horsepower. Packed into the agile STX sit-down hull to create the STX 310 model, the big motor lets riders rip across the water at 65 mph.

This drivetrain employs a 4-into-2-into-1 exhaust with dual water mufflers to minimize backpressure, maximizing the engine’s power and efficiency. The 160-mm jet pump has a three-blade impeller whose blade angles are optimized for peak acceleration and thrust.

Kawasaki let us ride the top-of-the-line STX 310RX, which lists for $20,199. There is a slightly less-well-equipped STX 310R that goes just as fast for $18,799. The test unit featured a 7-inch display panel containing the speedometer, tachometer, supercharger boost level, fuel level, trim setting, power mode setting, and compass. The rear-view camera on the STX lets the rider keep an eye on skiers, wakeboarders, or tube riders behind the watercraft.

We’ve gotten familiar with electronically controlled modes in modern cars, trucks, and motorcycles, and they are also present here in the Jet Ski STX 310RX. They are Smart Learning Operation (SLO), Lower Power Operation (LPO), Middle Power Operation (MPO), and Full Power Operation (FPO).

I started riding in MPO, thinking that would be a good get-acquainted scenario and I was pleasantly surprised at the STX 310’s speed. I guess I shouldn’t have been, considering that it has 310 horsepower. After a bit of that, I switched to FPO, and found the throttle response much touchier and acceleration quicker–perfect for big fun.

MPO limits peak power to 80 percent, while FPO unleashes all 310 horses. LPO makes the throttle response even more sluggish and further restricts maximum power to 60 percent. SLO mode requires a special yellow key and is aimed at true beginners, who, realistically, probably should be learning on something other than this supercharged beast.

Other gadgets include the Launch Control system, which automatically adjusts the jet pump’s trim over the course of an acceleration run, keeping it optimized as the boat’s attitude changes during the run. There’s also a handy one-touch 5-mph cruise control, good for complying with no-wake zones.

Hot-dogging on the STX is a good time, thanks to a hull design that was created for corner carving, without much risk of pitching the rider into orbit mid-corner. There are also some nice practical features, like a Neutral that preserves some degree of steering capability.

Jet Skis have no rudder, relying on thrust from the engine to steer them, so when the throttle is released, or the boat is shifted to neutral, you’d expect it to be adrift. But Kawasaki employs a thrust reverser that lets the STX simultaneously have no forward thrust while also having some steering capacity. That reverser also provides for a Reverse position that lets the ride back the STX.

Reverse is one of the amenities that led to the demise of original-style stand-up Jet Skis, which aren’t suited to such features. Kawasaki tried briefly to revive the format in 2017, but says that its new stand-up 2027 models are Back to the Future to stay this time.

I was pleasantly surprised to find that long-dormant stand-up riding skills were still sufficient for me to take off on the first try without falling.

Kawasaki offers two versions of its classic stand-up model for 2027, the Jet Ski SX-R 160 and SX-X 160. These are powered by 160-hp naturally aspirated versions of the 1.5-liter engine, with the difference between them being that the SX-R has a traditional-style moveable handlebar that starts off lying flat and the rider lifts it as they stand.

The SX-X has a fixed motorcross-style handlebar, giving riders a choice between the two styles. The test model was the SX-X motocrosser. I’d never ridden one like that before, but I found the fixed bar seemed to make it easier to pull myself up as the ski got underway.

However, after falling off, as one does on these things, you have to reach up from the water to reattach your wrist lanyard to the ignition interlock. This is the thing that shuts the ski off when you fall so that it doesn’t leave you behind, and you have to reconnect it to restart the machine.

But with the fixed bar up there pretty high from the water, I was happy to have my 35-inch sleeve length. Someone with more normal-length arms might find it hard to reach the switch while floating in the water alongside.

Just as I’d remembered stand-ups, the SX model is tremendously agile and fun for turns and jumps. And just as I remembered, it is easy to fall off in the process. Once it starts to roll onto its side, adding power might get you to ride out of it, or, as in my case, it might just make you hit the water while going even faster!

It doesn’t matter which handlebar style you prefer because both the SX-X 160 and SX-R 160 are $11,999. Getting one of these would allow you to cultivate some old-school riding skills while taking advantage of some throwback value. That was another key component of the original Pontiac GTO’s muscle car legend, so it is good to see in the Kawasaki showrooms for 2027.

#4598. EVgo opens its first Tesla Superchargers, with hundreds more planned

EVgo has opened its first Supercharger station, and it’s in a Chicago grocery store parking lot. The site has 12 fast-charging stalls with both NACS and CCS plugs, and it’s the first of hundreds of Tesla Supercharger stalls EVgo plans to add across the US.

The 325 kW “EVgo Superchargers” are at Riverside Square & River’s Edge, at 3145 S Ashland Avenue. EVgo’s August announcement cited up to 500 kW for the Supercharger rollout.

The Chicago location features Magic Dock technology, which means both NACS and CCS vehicles can charge without an adapter. Drivers of compatible non-Tesla EVs can start a session through the Tesla app. If you drive a Tesla, the charging station shows up in the car’s navigation and Trip Planner. Other EVgo fast chargers with NACS plugs have been showing up in Tesla navigation since early September if you turn on third-party charging.

“By serving both Tesla and non-Tesla NACS drivers, we’re doubling EVgo’s addressable market and continuing to meet EV drivers where they are and where they want to charge,” said Badar Khan, EVgo CEO.

EVgo owns the Superchargers and self-brands them, and Tesla runs and maintains them. The first sites will be at Regency Centers shopping plazas with grocery stores.

Smart move on EVGo's part. More reliable charger at a lower cost than they can build themselves, and Tesla takes on all the maintenance and network operations for a slice of the sales.

EVgo is also adding NACS plugs to its regular fast-charging network, a rollout it started in 2025. The company aims to have 500 of those stalls across the US by the end of 2026, with Supercharger stalls counted separately. Over the next two years, it plans to put at least one NACS plug at every EVgo site built in 2023 or later.

#4597. Tesla Cybertruck Production in Texas Is Ending, Elon Musk Says, Truck Seems Likely to Be Killed Off

The truck’s lead engineer is already referring to it in the past tense on X.

Tesla is “winding down” production of the Cybertruck in Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for additional Cybercab production, CEO Elon Musk says. As with so many other Tesla lineup announcements, the decision was announced in a tweet shared overnight. The Cybertruck’s lead engineer followed up with an X post of his own referring to the vehicle in the past tense, suggesting that the pickup will be axed rather than see production moved elsewhere.

It marks a fitting end for what was meant to be a major volume product for Tesla, one that was intended to fight the Ford F-150 and Chevrolet Silverado the same way that the more successful Model 3 and Model Y have long fought internal combustion sedans and crossovers across the world. The unusually-styled Cybertruck never became anything close to that kind of rainmaker for Tesla, even after Tesla introduced a cheaper, more basic model last year. Those results made this outcome almost inevitable.

The Cybertruck was revealed in November of 2019, but not delivered to customers until November of 2023. When the truck did arrive, it failed to hit the lofty range and price benchmarks that Tesla announced on stage at its initial reveal. With production now set to end in the middle of 2027, the gap between the reveal and release could end up being longer than the amount of time Tesla actually sold its flagship pickup.

Cybertrucks were recalled seven times in 2024 alone and again throughout its life cycle, most notably for risks of unintended acceleration and entire pieces of bare metal bodywork that could be shed at speed. In 2025, one owner shared a video of that piece flying off his truck with Road & Track.

Without the Cybertruck out, the Roadster set for a claimed 2028 release, and the Model S and Model X canceled, Tesla’s only current products will soon be the Model 3 and Model Y. Both have been major hits for Tesla, and both have received recent facelifts, but they will have to carry the brand’s showrooms on their own until Tesla can actually find a way to deliver its promised Cybercab.

#4596. Albatross couple George and Geraldine reunite for the 10th straight year

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

The Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii has welcomed a special couple: George and Geraldine, two short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus). The birds have officially found each other for nesting season on the Midway Atoll for the 10th straight year in a row.  George was first spotted on October 18, and the pair was reunited by October 22.

Every fall, the remote group of islands becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, including the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any current bird species. One Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis), on the other hand, claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird—the famous Wisdom, who is over 70 years old.

Short-tailed albatrosses (called makalena in Hawaiian) are almost completely white and feature a large pink bill. They can live up to 50 years, and as exemplified by George and Geraldine, are monogamous. They nest on islands and atolls, and the species is listed as endangered by both the United States government and the state of Hawaii. At the turn of the 20th century, feather hunting almost made the species go extinct.

“The vast majority of breeding for short-tailed albatross occurs on remote islands in the western Pacific, including Torishima Island, Japan, which is an active volcano south of Tokyo, and the Senkaku Islands near Taiwan,” according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). “Since 2000, biologists at the [Midway Atoll National Wildlife] refuge have used short-tailed albatross decoys and audio playback of the seabird’s calls to attract more of them.”

In fact, George and Geraldine are the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, though other members of their species were spotted last season. They were banded as chicks on Torishima Island and first seen together on Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in 2016. The cute pair brought their first chick into the world during the 2018-2019 breeding season.

“Millions of makalena once used their long wingspans to expertly glide on air currents across the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to Alaska and Hawaiʻi,” the FWS writes. “The slowly growing population is estimated at around 10,000 today.”

#4595. Hyundai’s $359 IONIQ 5 lease looks like a deal, but don’t overlook its bigger sibling

The Hyundai IONIQ 5 is the most popular EV in America outside of Tesla, but its larger three-row sibling looks like the better deal right now.

Through September, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 was the third top-selling EV in the US, behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3.

Hyundai’s electric SUV is outselling rivals like the Chevy Equinox EV, Ford Mustang Mach-E, and Toyota bZ.

Why? For one, it’s one of the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at about $35,000, and Hyundai has been offering some of the most attractive lease deals.

After the $7,500 federal EV tax credit expired at the end of September last year, Hyundai responded by reducing prices on the IONIQ 5 by up to nearly $10,000 on some trims.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250. That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. Upgrading to the extended-range SE RWD model adds $2,500, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

Hyundai’s three-row electric SUV, the IONIQ 9, starts at $58,955, or nearly $24,000 more than the base IONIQ 5 SE.

On Hyundai’s website, the 2027 IONIQ 5 SE Standard Range is available to lease from $359 a month. The offer is for a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing for an effective cost of $567 per month.

The extended-range Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE RWD can be leased from $369 a month. The offer is also a 24-month lease with $4,999 due at signing, for an effective cost of $577 per month.

Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9, meanwhile, is available to lease from $419 a month. That deal also includes $4,999 due at signing, but is for a 36-month lease, so the effective cost is $557 per month.

Using Hyundai’s payment calculator, it would cost about $412 a month to lease the 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 SE for 36 months with $4,999 due at signing. With an effective cost of $550 per month, it’s only $7 less than the three-row IONIQ 9.

The Hyundai IONIQ 9 offers more range than its smaller sibling, with an EPA-estimated range of up to 335 miles for the base SE trim.

The IONIQ 5 is a midsize electric SUV, about the same size as a Tesla Model Y, with two rows and enough room for five passengers. Hyundai’s larger IONIQ 9 offers three rows of seating and six- or seven-seat configurations.

With an added row of seating, the IONIQ 9 offers up to 163.54 cubic feet of interior passenger volume, compared with the IONIQ 5, which offers up to 106.5 cubic feet.

While the IONIQ 9 may be the better deal right now, the IONIQ 5 is still a good fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that doesn’t necessarily need the added space.

In comparison, the standard Tesla Model Y RWD is listed for lease starting at $499 a month with an EPA range of up to 321 miles. That’s for a 36-month lease with $3,000 down.

Using Tesla’s payment calculator, if you put the same $4,999 down for a 24-month lease like the IONIQ 5, the Model Y RWD’s monthly rate is $549.

Which one would you choose? The IONIQ 5, IONIQ 9, or Tesla Model Y? Let us know why in the comments.

Both the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are built at Hyundai’s Metaplant America outside of Savannah, Georgia.

I really haven’t seen much value in leasing. I’d rather buy the car outright using cash, with the goal of keeping the car for 10+ years.

When we toured the facility earlier this year, Hyundai told us that its electric SUVs are attracting new buyers to the brand at a higher rate than its gas or hybrid vehicles.

The IONIQ 5 had a 69.8% conquest rate last year, while the IONIQ 9 had 64.3%. Hyundai’s Elantra N ranked third (61.9%), followed by the Palisade (61.2%) and Kona Electric (60.9%).

#4593. Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

Published Nov 9, 2026 10:00 AM EST

Voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone. Actually, let’s call it a 16.09-billion-milestone. That’s the distance a photon can travel in a single day, which is to say the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be exactly one light-day away from our planet on November 18 at 5:18 a.m. EST.

At that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back. Imagine on a Friday morning telling your oven to turn on, but you don’t receive confirmation that it’s hot until Sunday. And by that point, the oven would have been baking whatever was inside for most of Saturday. That is the kind of delay that NASA’s Voyager team must work with.

Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S. Rankin tells Popular Science. Rankin is also a deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. “In my mind the fun is receiving a signal back from the Voyager, a light-day away.”

Rankin and other astronomers use those signals to study the very local interstellar medium, which is the suburb of space surrounding our solar system. Voyager 1 has been in this region, about 11 billion miles away, since 2012. There, the probe can detect changes in plasma and the magnetic field.

“Right now we’re trying to figure out how far out are the influences of the sun felt,” she says.

The sun continuously spits out charged particles in a stream of solar wind that extends into space. That wind pushes back against the gas and other interstellar stuff surrounding our solar system, sculpting a bubble in space known as the heliosphere. “There will be some part farther out, some distance away [where the] interstellar medium has no idea that the heliosphere is even there,” she says. Rankin adds that she thinks Voyager 1 is right on the edge of this “undisturbed, pristine interstellar medium.”

It is something of a marvel that the almost 50-year-old Voyager 1 continues to supply astronomers with data. To send information to Earth, the probe uses a 23-watt radio transmitter (about the output of a small refrigerator lightbulb). Only antennas as sensitive as the 70-meter-wide dishes in the NASA Deep Space Network can detect Voyager 1’s super-faint signal. Without them, the space probe would have gone incommunicado years ago.

When Voyager 1 launched in September 1977, the nuclear-powered spacecraft had 10 operational scientific instruments. It discovered new moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn on its way out of our solar system; its observations of Jupiter’s moon Europa hinted at a liquid ocean under an icy crust. When the probe traveled beyond our solar system’s planets, NASA’s Voyager team shut down unnecessary equipment to conserve power. Now only two of its instruments are active. Ongoing management continues to preserve as much juice as possible from the spacecraft’s dwindling plutonium supply. The team was also forced to turn off the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment in April. In September, NASA swapped out three systems for lower-power alternatives on the Voyager 1, about six weeks after the same strategy worked on its twin Voyager 2 probe.

“It’s fun to see what sort of innovation people come up with to keep the spacecraft going,” Rankin says. “There’s only so much you can turn off.”

Voyagers 1 and 2 have been operating without several instrument heaters for years. If shutting those off hadn’t worked, Rankin says “the mission would have ended a decade ago.”

Still, its operational margins are thin. In late October, NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1; that issue has appeared to resolve itself and may have been related to a group of thrusters going offline.

“This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in a news release. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” (JPL representatives did not respond to Popular Science’s requests for comment.)

All spacecraft missions must come to an end, no matter how plucky the probe or innovative its engineering team. NASA estimates that the Deep Space Network will lose contact with Voyager 1 around 2036, long before it travels to its two-light-day milestone. The probe may also freeze, unable to point properly back at Earth. Or its power systems will finally go kaput.

“We know that’s coming at some point. It’s probably not 20 years from now,” Rankin says. “It’s probably not 10 years from now.”

And then Voyager 1 will go forever radio silent as it cruises onward through the heavens.

#4592. Apollo’s newest electric scooter is also its lowest-cost yet

Apollo has spent the last several years carving out a spot for itself toward the more premium end of the electric scooter market. Now the company is trying something different: going after the mass market with its least expensive model yet.

The new Apollo Dash carries a $699 MSRP, but is launching at $599 as part of the company’s Black Friday sale running through November 30. More importantly, Apollo says the Dash isn’t intended to simply be a stripped-down budget scooter, but rather a way to bring much of its existing technology down to a lower price point.

The scooter uses a 48V electrical system powering a 600W nominal, 1,200W peak-rated Bosch motor, with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h). Its 480Wh battery is rated for up to 25 miles (40 km) of range in Eco mode.

Apollo also claims the 48V architecture avoids limiting motor power to anemic levels as the battery drains, meaning riders shouldn’t experience the same increasingly sluggish performance toward the bottom of the battery that can occur on some lower-cost scooters.

At 43 lb (19.5 kg), the Dash is reasonably portable, though getting the weight and price down comes with an important compromise: there’s no suspension. Apollo also caps rider weight at 220 lb (100 kg), and points heavier riders or those regularly tackling rough roads and hills toward the more expensive Apollo Go instead.

Despite the lower price, there’s still a surprisingly long feature list. The Dash gets IP66 water resistance, self-healing tubeless tires, regenerative braking, built-in turn signals, Apollo’s Beam stem light, NFC unlocking, Apple Find My integration, and connectivity with the Apollo smartphone app.

Apollo says it put the frame through 10,000 km (6,200 miles) of durability validation before shipping production units. A beta test program also accumulated 1,002 miles over 144 rides without any reported punctures or maintenance issues. Beta riders averaged 19 miles (30 km) per ride while finishing with 29% battery remaining, according to Apollo.

Perhaps the bigger story here, though, is where Apollo is positioning the Dash. The company says 52% of its customers previously owned scooters from brands including Segway, NIU, and Xiaomi, but historically moving up to an Apollo often meant crossing the $1,000 mark.

At $599, the Dash appears designed to get those riders into Apollo’s ecosystem much earlier – while also putting the company squarely into competition with the mass-market scooters it previously sat above.

And for those wanting a bit more power or features, Apollo’s more upmarket models are on sale now as part of early Black Friday promotions.
