#4529. Chunky mama bear wins 2026 Nope award for quick retreat from bigger rival

Published Nov 11, 2026 1:12 PM EST

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she said, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

Polestar revealed a Formula 2030 concept car at a media drive event for the Polestar 4, and while it’s not headed for production, the electric carmaker says some of its design language will preview the next-generation Polestar 2 as well as the upcoming Polestar 7. The four-door concept has a rear hatch and is unmistakably Polestar, as evident by the brand’s signature “Dual Blade” headlights and minimalistic design. However, its low-slung profile and flared rear fenders give it an aggressive, performance-oriented silhouette.

See all results for used Polestar for sale near 23917

The car’s coach doors remove the need for a B-pillar, and the A-pillar is disguised to give the windshield and windows a wrap-around effect. Interestingly, the concept has a single windshield wiper. Glass replaces a traditional roof, and the trunk gets a large window—a stark deviation from some of Polestar’s other windowless rear ends. The trunk’s floor is also transparent, and race-inspired Öhlins dampers peek through underneath.

Polestar calls the concept’s rear end “UFO-esque.” And instead of the single long light bar that angles downward on previous models, the concept car’s lighting signature is more subtle, with just two thin taillights located under the trunk.

Nitrogen, a new exterior color that debuts on the Formula 2030 concept, shows up in three different finishes around the exterior. Polestar’s tone-in-tone treatment uses a mix of glossy, matte, and satin finishes to distinguish details like the side cladding and aero bits. Even the 22-inch wheels are color-matched, with Swedish Gold-colored Brembo brake calipers as an accent.

Inside, the four-seater continues the tone-in-tone color scheme with light-colored upholstery and gold accents in the seatbelts and controls. The seats feature inflatable bolsters and cushions that mold themselves to each occupant, and most of the interior is composed of recycled materials.

Two screens—one attached to the steering column and one in the center of the dashboard—angle toward the driver, and eight physical controls lie in the center console below the larger screen. Drivers have options for each of the controls, both in what kind of tactile control it is, like a rocker switch or dial, and what function it affects.

The center console also houses a drive-mode selector where drivers can choose between Performance, Normal, and Autonomous modes. In Performance mode, the center screen lowers to sit flush with the center console while the steering wheel and gauge screen move closer to the driver. In Autonomous mode, the car’s concealed lidar unit appears outside the car while the steering wheel and driver’s seat move further apart inside the cabin.

#4527. The electric Vespa just got better where it actually matters

Vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.

But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.

Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.

The biggest upgrade is an entirely new electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.

On the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa says the new motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.

But perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the new removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.

The Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.

Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.

There’s also a new charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.

Vespa is clearly only really interested in selling their gas models, which come in 50cc, 125cc, & 310cc classes. And the only reason anyone would get a 50cc is if they didn't want to bother to get an actual motorcycle license in some jurisdictions. The electrics are nearly as expensive as the 310s but even the "faster" model only has the power equivalent of about 70cc's. At least the battery in the faster model is now a decent 4.2 kwh, though that one I believe is not removable. Hey I'm actually a Vespa lover I have a 200cc. They are beautiful quality machines, and I don't mind the price premium. But the electrics are quite disappointing, especially for the money. If they had a true 125cc equivalent I would be first in line at the showroom. Very disappointing in that a stouter motor really wouldn't cost them much more at all.

The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.

Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole update is how little of it you can actually see.

The company hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.

Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the new models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

#4526. Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

Published Nov 11, 2026 2:00 PM EST

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

“Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”

#4525. Nissan Dusts Off the ‘Patrol’ Badge for America With a New Off-Road Armada

Granted, the Armada Patrol Pro-4X is largely new in name alone, but we’re just happy to see that name back on our shores.

Nissan’s vehicles may not always come up in the top spot in comparison tests, but there’s one arena where the brand indisputably competes at the top rung in the United States: strong names. Pathfinder, Titan, Frontier, Rogue all ooze the toughness and attitude you want to identify with a truck or SUV. Leaf makes an electric vehicle’s eco-friendliness clear with a single syllable. Even Murano—named after fancy Italian glassware—suggests premium elegance in a way that, say, “RX450+” doesn’t.

And the 2027 Nissan Armada Patrol Pro-4X’s name makes it pretty, pretty clear that the company doesn’t have any intention of changing course anytime soon.

The new-for-’27 moniker marks the return of the “Patrol” badge to Nissan’s U.S. lineup after a 66-year absence, the nameplate last seeing the side of a vehicle in an American showroom the same year Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin planted their boots on the moon. It’s remained in widespread use elsewhere on Planet Earth, however, on several generations of burly body-on-frame sport-utility vehicles, including the one sold here as the Armada. That may mean the Armada Patrol name is sourced from the Department of Redundancy Department, but hey, we’re still happy to see it back.

Most of the rest of the SUV will be familiar to anyone who’s experienced the previous Armada Pro-4X off-road trim, as the new version is effectively a rebrand of that, but there are a couple other tweaks made for the 2027 model year. There’s a Nismo roof rack and Nismo rock sliders, as well as available Nismo Axis wheels wrapped in BFGoodrich off-road tires.

Otherwise, the new trim comes packing all the regular goodies previously found on a factory go-anywhere Armada. There’s the 3.5-liter twin-turbo V-6 making 425 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque, connected to a four-wheel drive system with electronic limited-slip differential and a 9-speed automatic gearbox. Adaptive air suspension, skid plate, off-road cameras and all-terrain tires all help it push further past the pavement than regular Armadas, while fender flares and red accents help set it apart visually.

Should you be interested in taking the 2027 Armada Patrol Pro-4x home—ideally by driving across a mountain range or two—you should plan on forking over at least $81,265 for the privilege. That’s $11,700 more than the starting price of a basic four-wheel drive Armada, but a few grand cheaper than its key rivals, the Ford Expedition Tremor and Chevrolet Tahoe Z71 with the 6.2-liter V-8. Also, with Detroit’s models, you can’t stand on the running board and make dad jokes about being “on patrol.”

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. A 12-year veteran of journalism, he formerly worked at Gear Patrol, The Drive, and RIDES Magazine, and contributed to the New York Daily News and Jalopnik, among other outlets. You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

#4524. Rewarding for the Right Owner: 1979 Lancia Zagato Tested

The car for those who view eccentricity as a virtue and fun as a necessity.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

“ZAG-uh-toe .... What is that, one of them new little Plymouths?”

He’d been studying the little Lancia through the window as we rummaged through his parts store in search of a you-wire-it cigarette lighter we could graft into the car’s electrical system. The on-board lighter socket had proved incompatible with our Escort’s plug.

“Za-GAH-toe,” we corrected. “It's made in Italy.”

He considered that piece of informa­tion as we paid for the lighter, then tried to sell us a can of engine additive as we made for the door. The dogeared display for the pour-in miracle claimed it would do everything short of putting you in the winner’s circle at Daytona. In the old days, in different packaging, it probably sold as a cure for rheumatism, lice, warts, heaves, halitosis, and hard hearing. He patted the uppermost can and his voice trailed us into the drizzly afternoon, hinting of impending doom.

See all results for used cars for sale near 36603

He had a point there, but we forsook the additive and let the door close be­hind us. We hooked up the Escort and set out into the growing evening rain­storm in search of a major mechanical or electrical failure to get pissed off about. The further we got from Dayto­na, spearing out into the chilly, desert­ed, water-swept two-lanes of central Florida, howling into the gloom at a steady 80, the clearer our second thoughts became. What if Lancia’s self­-incriminating talk of a “new high-quali­ty modular electrical system through­out” was just a hoax? We didn’t even have an umbrella. Would the modular electrics leave us sinking in the middle of some non-modular backwater swamp? Would the shift linkage come adrift? Would the carburetion cease to carburet, or the ignition cease to ignite? These were fits of pique visited upon us by Lancias before. But the Zagato did none of the above. Oh, the letdown, not to be able to tell you we had to hitch­hike out of the Glades in the back of a sagging half-ton Ford pickup.

Times have apparently changed at Lancia. While we can’t say the thrashing we dealt our Zagato was the equivalent of 50,000 miles’ worth of normal driv­ing, the car suffered us, if not gladly, at least with no crippling catastrophes. Its shortcomings fell more in the area of nuisance value, an area offset by the fun of driving the car under the right cir­cumstances. As often happens with cars of strong character, the Zagato’s car-to-­owner-to-car relationship becomes a high-spirited adversary relationship, an exchange of sometimes conflicting, sometime parallel philosophies. This re­lationship can make a Lancia Zagato a rewarding car for the right owner. All that remains is to determine whether ownership then qualifies him as a 24-ka­rat eccentric in good standing, or simply a lover of good fun.

See all results for used cars for sale near 36603

Fun is what Lancia had in mind when it contracted Carrozzeria Zagato to cre­ate and build a coachbuilt steel targa body for the existing Beta Coupe. The unit-bodied result is an interesting com­bination of a normal lift-off fiberglass targa roof panel and an everyday roadster’s fold-down vinyl rear roof and plastic window. The targa bar that re­mains after everything else is lifted off or folded down provides sturdy rollover protection, enhanced by horizontal out­er roofline struts that connect the bar with the windshield pillars. Four configurations are possible by adding or re­moving the roof components and roll­ing windows up or down.

The resulting greenhouse possesses all the elegance of a railroad shanty and thwarts the clean, simple lines of the lower body. From certain angles, the Zagato looks like a stubby El Camino pickup with an enclosed bed, but unlike an El Camino, it has another pair of seats behind the driver and the number­-one passenger. However, candidates for travel in back may want to suggest a democratic drawing of straws, fearing their upper and lower extremities will be forever molded into unnatural shapes. Lowering the back window pro­vides a modern version of the rumble seat and a bit more headroom, but no extra sympathy for the legs. The Zagato is not by any means or intent an appro­priate way to transport half your neigh­borhood to a formal dinner party. Con­sider it a sports car that happens to ben­efit from a slight extra people-carrying capacity suited to quick runs down to the beach, the movies, or the local wa­tering hole.

As always, Lancia has provided a nice setting for front-seat travelers, creating a modern environment that welcomes you with comfort—though the passen­ger is probably more comfortable than the driver. The seats are good, but the driver is squeezed into the classic Amer­ican-knees-in-the-American-armpits Italian driving position, arms stretching for a steering wheel that lies out near the horizon.

But inside the car, you tend to forget about the varied points of styling and sometimes even about the peculiar driv­ing position. Sometimes the Zagato is so much fun you can’t help yourself. Other people watch you rip past, and you know they’re thinking, “What would I do if I had that? What does it feel like without a roof or a back win­dow?” They figure anything with these looks must be kinda fast, and they won­der how many friends you can squeeze into the thing before the cops stop you. The Zagato is meant for the unpredict­able kind of fun you can have only if you’re unpredictable enough to have a car like this. If that’s eccentric, so be it.

The Zagato’s chassis configuration has become so commonplace as to have lost all appeal for eccentrics. Contained within the 92.5-inch wheelbase and 164.6-inch overall length are the trans­verse engine and front-wheel drive shared with Lancia’s other models, and echoed by a dozen other manufacturers. A five-speed manual or a new three-­speed automatic transmission provides the gearing, and the engine, provided by parent company Fiat, has been en­larged for all Lancia’s models this year, jumping from 1756 cc to 1995 cc. The 84.0 mm bore remains the same, but the stroke has been increased from 79.2 to 90.0 mm. The two-liter whips out 87 horsepower at an enthusiastic 5400 rpm and boasts a torque increase of almost 17 percent, up to 105 pound-feet at 2900 rpm. The double-overhead-cam four leans over twenty degrees, and its electronic ignition, Weber two-barrel carburetor, and aluminum hemi-heads provide both exotic specifications and good midrange performance. The en­gine runs on unleaded gas, purifies its wastes with a catalytic converter, and, when hitched to the five-speed over­drive, propels the Zagato an average of 19 miles per gallon.

At 2730 pounds, the Zagato is heavy for a car its size. Its standard high nu­merical gearing is necessary for lively around-town and back-road perform­ance, but it produces much noisy com­plaint from the engine in the lower gears. Fourth gear above 60 is hopelessly noisy even though it has another 27 mph worth of revs left. Fifth ceases the caterwauling up to about 70 mph, when droning sets in and wind noise around the roof panel and rear window increas­es to what seem supersonic levels. Noisy and tightly wound though it might be, the wailing little engine produces only mid-pack performance—0 to 60 mph in 11.9 seconds, the quarter-mile in 18.7 seconds at 73 mph. By standing on the gas long enough, you can wring a 103-mph top speed out of the Zagato. Its passing performance is quite reassuring when you’ve picked the right gear. On occasion, getting the right gear can be much more a bother than picking it, but the transaxle’s linkage isn’t entirely bad, and the fat shift knob and easy heel­-and-toe movement are fine. The five­-speed pattern is a proper H, with fifth up and away, opposite reverse.

The brakes Lancia has hung under the coachwork are more than just reas­suring. With a big disc at every hand­some alloy wheel, and aggressive, low­-profile Pirelli P6s, the Zagato likes nothing better than knocking off speed with breathtaking quickness and control. The speedometer needle struggles to keep up in getting down. Pedal effort is light, and the rousing 186-foot mea­surement for 70-to-0-mph stops runs neck-and-neck with or even betters some of the world’s highest-performance automobiles.

The 185/65R-14 P6 Pirellis are tre­mendous. Not only do they ride smoothly and quietly, even at the high pressures we use for hard running, they’re beyond reproach in their per­formance characteristics. They are pre­dictable, precise, and monumental in their ability to inspire confidence. They seem to have no sudden tuck-under, and finding their limit seems almost as much a mental exercise as a physical one. While the Pirellis are good, the Za­gato certainly adds its own zesty spice to the handling brew. The spring and shock rates provide a firm smoothness of control. The car’s aloof road man­ners do not disappear into the lower re­cesses of every chuckhole or flutter over every sudden rise. The suspension is all-independent, MacPherson struts all around. Each aspect of wheel control is dovetailed neatly with the others, from the point where the P6s manhandle the pavement right up to the precise, re­fined new rack-and-pinion power steer­ing, which allows only slight tugs on the wheel in the lower gears. If it were not for the power assist, the awkwardly positioned steering wheel would be a real obstacle, more opponent than ac­complice in the battle of leverage. Its rake adjustment allows none of the fore­-and-aft movement so badly needed for correct reach to the wheel.

Directional stability is outstanding, the Zagato arrowing its way over and through every snide parlor trick our grousing malcontent of a highway system can throw at it. The inherent understeer is moderate, and its symptoms are fur­ther reduced by the quick steering and the response of the Pirellis. Body roll and brake dive are under tight rein. The car works not as a scurvy rat's nest of separate parts, but as one very snug unit.

Lancia hasn’t been exactly famous for well-conceived interiors, but the Zagato benefits from a general redesign for 1979. Our white test car, trimmed in black and sporting the new bumpers and restyled grille and hood introduced this year on the older Beta Coupe, was cloaked inside with gray cut-pile carpet and black leather. The dash, also black, contains a new, six-gauge instrument panel. A 120-mph speedometer and a 7000-rpm tachometer, redlined at 6500, dominate the scene, even though they’re partly hidden behind the over­styled wheel, which has miserably placed spokes. Smaller gauges keep tabs on amps, fuel, and water temp, the oth­er three being allotted to the oil pres­sure, temperature, and level. Our water­-temp gauge wasn’t registering, so that must have meant we didn't have any . . . what, water or temp? The layout is clut­tered around the nacelle for the radio (which is very good and has a power an­tenna), but the general ergonomics and labeling of controls are excellent. The ventilation, heater, and air conditioning worked very well, handling unexpected Florida extremes in a manner obtrusive only because such adroitness was a sur­prise in a newly introduced limited-pro­duction car.

Several irritating bugaboos crop up here and there around the Zagato to take the edge off the nicer sides of its personality. A horrid “modesty panel” (the biz name for the under-dash trim panel that hides a car’s plumbing and wiring woes from critical eyes) snaps at your toes every time you press the clutch pedal, solidly and dangerously snagging your shoe as you let the pedal back out. The sun visors cannot be fold­ed to the sides. The shoulder harness has a tendency to tangle. The plastic rear window is clouded with a chemical haze. The rear-view mirror vibrates. The glove-box door fits poorly and is blemished with a bright blue “Unleaded Fuel Only” badge. And the hardware and trim don’t equal the excellent over­all paint and finish.

The Zagato, at a base price of $10,811, is about 1300 clams up on the Beta Coupe from which it springs. If its price isn’t enough to guarantee exclu­sivity to the eccentrics in its future, its availability will be: fewer than 1500 Za­gatos will be sold here. For those who can’t bear the thought of showing up at the same party with identical designer originals, a Special Edition Zagato, gild­ed in black paint, gold striping, unique emblems, and black interior, will be marketed at $11,800. Only 250 of these will find their way in.

Now all the U.S. Lancia dealers have to do is find a crowd of young, wind-in-­the-hair eccentrics who like to have fun driving fast with a carload of outdoorsy blondes over perfectly awful roads that don’t demand a lot of horsepower. Piece of cake. But they should beware of a potential buyer who sidles up looking for one of them new little Plymouths. He really just wants to unload some en­gine additive that, in a pinch, can cure hard hearing, halitosis, heaves, warts, lice, and rheumatism.

We checked every price and stock status in this post on Barnes & Noble Wednesday afternoon, November 11.

B&N lists it as a 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray combo, so the standard disc covers any player in the house that can’t handle 4K. The bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and they play on any Blu-ray player or game console with a disc drive. The KPop Demon Hunters Blu-ray is $19.99 and the KPop Demon Hunters DVD is $14.99, though its 4K edition is out of stock online. Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite is also $19.99.

#4521. 1.2 Million Ford Explorers Under Federal Probe Over Reports of 3rd-Degree Burns from Airbags

The seat-mounted side airbags ⁠have allegedly caused serious ​injuries, including to law enforcement officers.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened a probe into 1.2 million Ford Explorer vehicles over allegations that seat-mounted side airbags have accidentally deployed and given passengers third-degree burns.

NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation opened the investigation on Friday, November 6, after receiving eight Vehicle Owner Questionnaires and four Early Warning Reporting “Death and Injury” reports describing burn injuries following side airbag deployment in model year 2021-2026 Ford Explorer vehicles. The reports claim that crashes involving deployment of the seat-mounted side airbag have resulted in second- or third-degree burns for both drivers and front passengers.

Many law enforcement agencies across the country have adopted the Ford Explorer Police Interceptor as their vehicle of choice. As a result, NHTSA has received reports of injuries to law enforcement officers. A total of 10 injuries have been reported to the federal safety regulator.

A preliminary investigation has been opened, and the Office of Defects Investigation will evaluate the scope, frequency, and potential safety-related consequences of the alleged defect.

“Safety is a top priority at Ford. We are working with NHTSA to support its investigation,” a Ford spokesperson said to Road & Track.

#4520. Toyota sells 3 electric SUVs, but which one is best for you?

Toyota now offers three fully electric SUVs: the bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland. Here’s how they stack up.

After introducing the new and improved bZ (formerly the bZ4X) in late 2025, the electric SUV quickly became one of the most popular EVs in the US.

In the first nine months of 2026, it was the fourth-best-selling electric vehicle, behind the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

With two additional electric SUVs now on sale, the CH-R and bZ Woodland, Toyota has suddenly become one of America’s top-selling EV brands.

Its EV sales have nearly tripled this year. According to Cox Automotive, Toyota ranked as the third most popular EV brand behind Tesla and Rivian in the third quarter.

Toyota offers three distinct electric vehicles: the 2027 bZ, C-HR, and bZ Woodland, each designed for different lifestyles, so which one is the best fit for you?

After launching the updated model last year, the 2027 bZ starts at $34,980. With the $1,595 delivery fee, the starting price is $36,576.

That’s for the standard 2027 Toyota bZ XLE FWD with an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 236 miles. For longer range, you can upgrade to the FWD Plus model, which offers up to 314 miles and starts at $37,980 (excluding the delivery fee).

The Toyota bZ is available in XLE and Limited grades, with front- or all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrains.

Two battery options are offered: The 57.7 kWh battery on the standard XLE FWD provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 236 miles, while the larger 74.7 kWh battery provides up to 288 miles of range on the XLE AWD and 314 miles on the XLE FWD Plus model.

FWD models produce either 165 hp (XLE FWD) or 221 hp (XLE FWD Plus and Limited FWD), while AWD models deliver a combined 338 hp.

The 2027 bZ also has a built-in NACS port, so you can use Tesla Superchargers without needing a separate adapter. Toyota said it takes around 30 minutes to charge the battery from 10% to 80%.

Inside, the 2027 bZ features Toyota’s updated cabin design. The setup features a 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and a new 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The bZ is essentially designed as an everyday driver with a long driving range, modern tech, and available AWD.

For those looking for a bigger, more rugged option, the 2027 bZ Woodland may be a better fit. The Woodland is 6″ longer than the standard bZ and comes with standard AWD.

The longer body opens up more interior space, with up to 74.3 cubic feet of storage compared to the bZ with up to 67.1 cubic feet.

Unlike the bZ, the Woodland model has a standard AWD powertrain with Toyota’s X-Mode control system.

The setup delivers a combined 375 horsepower, 37 hp more than the standard bZ, making it Toyota’s most powerful EV currently.

It also adopts a more commanding, upright stance with 8.3″ of ground clearance and 3,500 lbs of towing capacity.

Although it uses the same 74.7 kWh battery as the standard bZ, the Woodland’s EPA-estimated range drops to 281 miles because of the added weight and power. Upgrading to the optional all-terrain tires sacrifices even more range, with up to 260 miles.

Like the bZ, the Woodland also has a built- in NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes.

Inside, the bZ Woodland features the same 7″ LCD customizable Multi Information Display (MID) and 14″ Toyota Audio Multimedia display screen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380. All variants include standard roof rails, Dual Qi-capable wireless device chargers, heated front seats and steering wheel, and Digital Key capabilities.

Last, but not least, the C-HR is a smaller, sporty, coupe-like electric SUV. The 2027 Toyota C-HR starts at $37,080, or $2,100 more than the standard bZ.

It’s about 6.7″ shorter than the bZ, with a smaller wheelbase, but also comes with standard AWD. The dual-motor AWD setup delivers a combined 338 hp, not quite as much as the bigger, more powerful Woodland.

The C-HR is available exclusively with the 74.7 kWh battery, which provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 287 miles for the SE grade with 18″ wheels.

Upgrading to 20″ wheels adds a street-ready look but offers slightly less EPA range, with up to 273 miles.

The coupe-like design adds a sleek look and opens up interior space, with up to 59.5 cubic feet of rear cargo space when the rear seats are folded. That’s slightly more than the bZ, which offers up to 56.9 cubic feet.

Inside, the C-HR features the same setup as its other EVs, including a 7″ slim driver’s display and 14″ central infotainment screen.

Like Toyota’s other electric SUVs, the C-HR has a native NACS port. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes about 30 minutes.

These are all basically the same small vehicles. I did not fit in any of them (6’ 2”) it is so frustrating to have less than 300 miles of range on AWD versions that are supposed to be better models.

It is 2026 over a decade since EVs arrived and over 5 years after the Tesla Model Y with practically zero competition almost at same price (Rivian R2 may be next year when affordable versions ship.) BMW, Mercedes and Volvo need $10k more. Hyundai has kept EV5 out of USA.

It is almost like none of the Legacy automakers want any SUV that can compete on price.

The 2027 Toyota C-HR EV is available in two trims: SE and XSE. Standard features include two wireless Qi phone chargers, low-profile roof rails, Fabric/SofTex-trimmed seating, heated front seats and steering wheel, Toyota Safety Sense 3.0, and a power liftgate.

#4519. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

#4517. The Mercedes-Benz EQS drove 539 miles on a single charge. Still worried about range?

The new Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ covered 539 miles without stopping to charge, making range anxiety look like a thing of the past.

Mercedes-Benz overhauled the EQS electric sedan, including a bigger battery and an 800V electrical architecture.

The 2027 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ uses a 122 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 467 miles.

While that’s already impressive, the electric sedan will likely go even farther in everyday driving conditions. During Edmunds recent EV Range Test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ drove a whopping 539 miles without stopping to charge.

The EQS beat its own EPA estimate by 72 miles and is now the longest-range electric sedan Edmunds has ever tested, beating the Lucid Air, the first EV to break the 500-mile mark. The only EV that has it beat is the Cadillac Escalade IQ, which managed 558 miles from its massive 205 kWh battery.

During the test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ was also more efficient than its official numbers suggest.

The new EQS used 29.6 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 28 kWh per 100 miles. In comparison, the 2025 Mercedes EQS 450+ covered 464 miles and used 34 kWh per 100 miles during the same test, so the improvements are considerable.

Edmunds observed a peak charging rate of 350 kW, in line with Mercedes’ estimates, while it sustained an average of 222 kW throughout the session.

Both beat the older EQS, which reached a peak charge rate of 208 kW and sustained an average of 175 kW.

The new Mercedes EQS 450+ added 825 miles of range in an hour, and 100 miles in just over 7 minutes, nearly twice the speed of the 2025MY.

The Edmunds EV Range Test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions. It includes 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

How much is too much? 539 miles on a single charge is impressive, but do you need it? In a recent “nationally representative” survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study showed that 73% consider 25, 50, or 75 miles enough to cover their daily driving. However, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range before they would consider an EV.

If you have access to a home charger, nothing beats waking up with a full charge every day. Meanwhile, public charging continues to improve, giving EV drivers more reliable options on longer trips.

Faster charging also helps. Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in around 10 minutes.

In the same Edmunds EV Range Test last week, the new 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive drove 436 miles on a single charge, exceeding its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles. It also used 28.3 kWh per 100 miles during the test, beating its official EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles.

I'm really glad to see more articles like this and people talking more about efficiency. It's not just about bigger batteries and range. It needs to be about smaller batteries plus great efficiency giving that same range. We need to do this with more efficient designs, more sedans and lighter vehicles.

The new 2027 Volvo EX60 drove 352 miles while the 2027 Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric covered 392 miles during the same test.

One thing is certain: electric vehicles are becoming more efficient, enabling longer driving ranges and faster charging times. As battery tech advances, EVs will drive farther and charge faster, while safety and performance will continue to improve.

How much driving range would you consider enough for your daily drive? What about for the week? Let us know in the comments below.

Want to play with dogs at the airport and have it be for a good cause? Well, boy, do we have the volunteer gig for you. It’s actually less playtime and more very serious Transportation Security Administration (TSA) work, but there’s still dogs, so we consider that a win: The TSA is currently looking for volunteers to be explosive detection K9 decoys, and honestly there may not be a cuter way to spend a weekend. Let these very smart dogs show us all just how smart they really are!

You also have to be comfortable sitting, walking, and moving around an airport. However, wheelchair and scooter users can participate in the program.

You can check out their annual calendar, which will be available in November or December. A German shorthaired pointer named Bolt won the TSA’S Cutest Canine Contest for 2026 and will be one of the working dogs featured on the 2027 calendar.

#4515. Hyundai Facing Class-Action Lawsuit Over Driver Monitoring System's Alleged False Alarms

According to the lawsuit, Hyundai knew its driver monitoring cameras had issues, but suggested drivers try fixes like different eyeglasses.

Automakers are constantly striving to make cars safer. New technologies such as automatic emergency braking, lane-keep assist, and driver monitoring systems were all developed to prevent crashes. However, according to a recent class-action lawsuit, one of those technologies designed to keep us out of trouble may be causing more trouble than it’s worth.

According to ClassAction.org, a 70-page complaint filed September 16 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California alleges that Hyundai's Direct Driver Monitoring System (DDMS) in the 2024-2026 Hyundai Santa Fe, 2025-2026 Ioniq 5, 2025-2026 Tucson, 2025-2026 Santa Cruz, and 2026 Palisade incorrectly identifies attentive drivers as distracted. The plaintiffs argue that this goes far beyond simple annoying warning messages, as the vehicles could also disable the cruise control system and even trigger unexpected automatic braking.

The logic behind Hyundai's DDMS is sound. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 315,167 people were injured by distracted driving in 2024 alone. Hyundai is attempting to reduce this number by using their DDMS to check for signs of distracted driving, with the setup working with the Forward Attention Warning (FAW) system to monitor the driver’s eyes, face and head position using a camera. When it detects what it believes to be distracted driving, it will alert the driver; if the system repeatedly detects an inattentive driver while cruise control is engaged, it can deactivate cruise control and initiate an emergency stop, bringing the vehicle to a halt.

But several Hyundai owners claim the DDMS is flagging drivers who are fully alert and paying attention to the road. According to the plaintiffs in this case, Hyundai knew about this potential flaw nearly two years ago when the company issued technical service bulletin 25-GI-001H in January 2025. According to the lawsuit, Hyundai’s proposed solution to the problem was that drivers “need to wear different sunglasses or glasses, adjust their seats, and look at the road.”

The lawsuit states that Hyundai's own owner's manuals acknowledge that its driver monitoring system may malfunction under a surprisingly wide range of normal driving conditions: wearing sunglasses, prescription glasses, heavy makeup, or a hat can interfere with the camera; so can bright sunlight, laughing, squinting, turning your head, or simply being too tall or too short. Even a bumpy road or the position of your hands on the steering wheel can reportedly confuse the system. (In other words, quite a few things people routinely do while driving could potentially trigger false warnings.)

The lawsuit seeks damages and other relief for affected Hyundai owners, but the allegations have yet to be proven in court.

#4514. PlugShare finally adds dark mode, and there’s more for EV drivers

PlugShare is giving its EV charging app a big overhaul. Version 8.0 arrives worldwide for iPhone on November 10, with dark mode, a trip planner that shows how far apart charging stops are, and a rebuilt Apple Watch app that can point you to a charger compatible with your EV.

Dark mode was one of the most-requested features from PlugShare users. It works across the app and follows your iPhone’s settings, so if your phone switches to dark mode at sunset, your charging map will, too.

The trip planner gets a small but handy change. Each charging stop now shows how far it is from both the start of your trip and the previous stop. So when you’re deciding whether to stretch to the next fast charger or stop sooner, the number you need is right there.

PlugShare now loads your saved locations, trips, and profile when you open the app or sign in, so those tabs are ready to tap. You can also open and zoom in on station photos right from their thumbnails. That’s handy when you’re trying to figure out what corner a charging station is in in a big parking lot. The app also adapts its layout to the iPhone Duo’s different screens and folded positions.

The rebuilt Watch app lists nearby charging stations with distances and directions. It uses the filters you’ve set on your iPhone, so if you’ve filtered for plugs that fit your EV, that carries over to your wrist.

Tap a station and you’ll see its PlugScore, the network that runs it, a small map, and which plugs it has, including NACS, CCS, CHAdeMO, or J1772. The list refreshes when you raise your wrist and open the app. You can also add a shortcut to a round or corner slot on your watch face.

The iPhone update is rolling out through the App Store. PlugShare says Android users will get dark mode and a redesign based on Google’s Material 3 in early 2027.

#4513. 2026 kitchen gift guide: Essential cooking gear for chefs of every level

Updated Nov 11, 2026 10:48 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

You don’t have to be great at cooking to enjoy it. Having the right gear really helps, though, and that creates a wellspring of great gifting opportunities. The HORL3 Cruise holds a knife against a magnet at a fixed 15- or 20-degree angle while a diamond disc rolls along the edge. The ThermoWorks Thermapen Nano gets a reading in about 0.4 seconds, so you can stop guessing when a roast is done. The Challenger Bread Pan traps steam under a tall cast-iron lid, the same trick bakeries pull off with steam-injected ovens. Every pick below works on that principle, from a $16 three-pack of Swiss peelers to a $750 Ankarsrum stand mixer whose bowl spins on top of the motor instead of under a beater.

There are 65 gifts here, grouped by category. Jump to: precision and measurement, knives and sharpening, pans and cookware, coffee, tea and drinks, baking and from scratch, countertop appliances, prep and storage, pantry and stocking stuffers.

Seasoning a thick steak with a typical pepper grinder takes a lot of twisting. The MÄNNKITCHEN Pepper Cannon uses hardened high-carbon stainless steel burrs spinning on a drive shaft supported by two bearings inside a body milled from a solid block of anodized aluminum. MÄNNKITCHEN claims 10 times the output of top-rated mills, which it describes as seven cranks instead of 70. You set the grind from 8 to 60+ mesh with an adjuster on the base that clicks into spring-loaded detents. The hopper holds half a cup of peppercorns, and a removable cup underneath catches up to a third of a cup of ground pepper, which is handy when a rub calls for a measured amount.

A big mixing bowl tends to hide a kitchen scale’s display right when you need to read it. On the OXO Good Grips 11 lb Stainless Steel Food Scale with Pull-Out Display, the readout sits on a tray that slides out from the base, clear of whatever’s on the platform, then tucks back in for storage. It weighs up to 11 pounds (5 kilograms), and a meter on the display shows how much capacity you have left as you add ingredients. The display has an optional backlight, and the stainless steel platform lifts off so you can wash it by hand.

Sous vide cooking holds a water bath at the exact temperature you want your food to finish at, so a steak can sit in it and stay medium-rare instead of drifting toward well-done. The Anova Precision Cooker 3.0 heats that bath with an 1,100-watt element and circulates 8 liters of water per minute, and Anova rates it to hold within 0.2°F anywhere from 32°F to 197°F. A two-line touchscreen on the cooker shows time and temperature, and dual-band Wi-Fi lets you start or check a cook from your phone. Anova gives it an IPX7 water-resistance rating, and the clamp adjusts and detaches to fit different pots.

ThermoWorks has closed out the Thermapen One, and the Thermapen Nano took its place this year. ThermoWorks rates the Nano’s fixed thermocouple probe for a full reading in 0.4 seconds and accuracy within 0.5°F between -4°F and 248°F, a window that covers everything from rare beef to pulled pork. Two magnets built into the body let it ride on the side of the fridge or range hood, and the display rotates a full 360 degrees, so the numbers read right-side up whichever hand you hold it in. It’s IP67 rated, runs roughly 1,000 hours on one AAA battery, and comes with a five-year warranty and a NIST-traceable calibration certificate.

A fast thermocouple thermometer doesn’t have to cost triple digits. TempPro, the brand formerly known as ThermoPro, builds a thermocouple sensor into the TempSwift Pro TP622 and rates it for a 0.1-second response time and accuracy within 0.5°F across -58°F to 572°F. That high end reaches past meat into frying oil and candy-making territory. The backlit display auto-rotates 180 degrees for left- or right-handed use, and the thermometer wakes up when you lift it and goes to sleep after 90 seconds of sitting still. It carries an IP65 water-resistance rating and runs on a single AAA battery.

The Combustion Predictive Thermometer (2nd Gen) is built around the question people actually ask during a roast: how much longer? Its probe carries eight sensors along its length, so the app can show the core, the surface and the air temperature around the food at the same time. Combustion’s prediction engine uses that heat-flow data to estimate the time remaining, and a feature it calls TrueCore reports the lowest internal reading even if you didn’t hit the center. Combustion rates the upper half of the probe to 900°F, so it can stay in a roast under the broiler or on the grill. Bluetooth reaches more than 330 feet in open air, and Wi-Fi requires a separate booster accessory.

Freehand sharpening is hard mostly because holding a steady angle is hard. The HORL3 Cruise takes that job off your hands: a magnetic block holds the knife at either 15 or 20 degrees, and you roll a wheel with a diamond disc back and forth along the edge. The other end of the roller carries a stainless steel honing disc to straighten and refine the edge you just ground. The Cruise’s body is made from ocean-bound recycled plastic, and HORL builds it in Germany. If the person you’re shopping for would rather have wood on the counter, the $179 HORL3 uses an oak or walnut body and swaps in an interchangeable ceramic disc.

STEELPORT forges its 8-inch Chef Knife from a single billet of American 52100 carbon steel in Portland, Oregon, then heat treats the edge and spine differently. The company says the edge ends up around 65 HRC, hard enough to take and hold a fine edge, while the spine stays below 30 HRC so the blade as a whole is less brittle. The handle is resin-stabilized Oregon bigleaf maple burl, and a magnetic walnut sheath comes in the box. Carbon steel picks up a patina and can rust, so wipe it dry after every wash. STEELPORT covers the knife with a lifetime warranty and sharpens it free for as long as you own it.

A knife that suddenly feels dull often has an edge that’s just rolled over, and a few passes on a honing rod push it back into line between real sharpenings. STEELPORT’s 12-Inch Oval Ceramic Honing Rod does that with a fine-grit ceramic surface over a steel core. The oval cross-section is there for contact, and STEELPORT says it puts more of the blade against the rod than a round one does. The rod measures 17 inches overall with a 5-inch contoured walnut handle and a finger guard, and it weighs 12 ounces. Ceramic can crack if it hits a tile floor, so give it a hook or its own drawer slot.

Shun builds the Classic 8-Inch Chef’s Knife around a VG-MAX steel core clad in 34 layers of stainless Damascus on each side, which is where the rippled pattern on the blade comes from. The core is hardened to 60-61 on the Rockwell scale and hand-sharpened to about 16 degrees per side, a fine edge that slices through onions and herbs cleanly. The full-tang blade sits in a D-shaped black PakkaWood handle, and the whole knife weighs 7.5 ounces. Shun makes it in Seki, Japan. A hard, thin edge like this one is happiest on a wood or plastic board, and it shouldn’t go anywhere near bones or frozen food.

Softer stainless steel is quicker to bring back to a sharp edge, and that’s part of the appeal of the Made In 8-Inch Chef Knife. It’s fully forged in Thiers, France, from nitrogen-treated X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58+ HRC, so a few passes on a whetstone or rolling sharpener refresh it. Made In grinds the edge asymmetrically, with a 14-degree primary bevel on one side and a 4-degree polishing bevel on the other, for 18 degrees total. The blade actually measures 8.5 inches and the knife weighs 7 ounces. If you order directly from Made In, the company will engrave it for $30 more, but engraved knives can’t be returned.

Someone outfitting a first real kitchen needs a handful of good knives more than a block with 15 slots. The Cangshan N1 Series 6-Piece Knife Block Set forges its blades from German X50CrMoV15 stainless hardened to 58 HRC, a steel that’s easy to touch up at home. The N1’s signature is its patented all-metal hollow handle, which runs straight out of the blade, so there are no wood or plastic scales to crack or loosen. Cangshan sells the set under more than one model number, so check the knife list on the listing before you order.

Tojiro has renamed its long-running DP line to Classic, but the F-808 210mm gyuto itself didn’t change. It’s a san mai blade, with a VG10 stainless core hardened to about 60 HRC sandwiched between softer stainless outer layers that add toughness around the hard cutting steel. The 50/50 double-bevel edge suits right- and left-handed cooks equally, and the Western-style handle has a full tang, a stainless bolster and three rivets, so it’ll feel familiar to anyone coming from a German knife. Tojiro makes it in Tsubame-Sanjo, Japan. The edge measures 212 millimeters and the knife weighs 7.2 ounces.

Learning to sharpen on a stone starts with two grits, and the King KW-65 puts both on one block. The 1000-grit side does the sharpening and raises a fresh edge, then the 6000-grit side polishes it. It’s a soaking stone, so you submerge it for a couple of minutes before you start and keep it wet while you work. The muddy slurry that builds up on the surface helps it cut, so leave it there rather than rinsing it away mid-session. The stone measures about 7.3 by 2.5 by 1 inches, sits in an included plastic stand, and is made in Japan.

The deep, 6-quart sauté pan at the center of the All-Clad NS Pro Ceramic Nonstick VIP comes with a steamer insert, a roasting rack and a tempered glass lid, so one piece of cookware can sear and steam on the stovetop or roast in the oven. The body is hard-anodized recycled aluminum, and a stainless steel base bonded underneath makes it work on induction burners. The ceramic nonstick interior is oven-safe to 450°F, though the lid tops out at 350°F and the pan can’t go under the broiler. Wash it by hand, and know that All-Clad’s warranty on this pan runs one year.

Carbon steel seasons and sears like cast iron, and it heats up and cools down faster when you adjust the burner. Made In’s Seasoned Carbon Steel Frying Pan arrives pre-seasoned with shea nut and coconut oils, so you can start cooking in it sooner than you could with a bare pan. The 12-inch size weighs 4.31 pounds, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2.25-inch sides. Made In builds it in Sweden, rates it for heat up to 1,200°F, and says it works on induction and over an open fire. The hollow stainless handle is designed to stay cool, and the pan should be washed by hand and dried right away.

Smithey is better known for cast iron, but its Deep Farmhouse Skillet is hand-forged carbon steel, made in Charleston, South Carolina. It’s about 12 inches across the top and 2 inches deep, which leaves room for a pan sauce or a shallow fry, and the cooking surface measures about 9.5 inches. Long handles on both sides stretch it to almost 21 inches end to end, so you can carry all 6 pounds of it to the table with two hands. Smithey lists it for use on gas, induction, electric and open fire.

Smithey’s 7.25 QT Dutch Oven skips enamel entirely. It’s bare cast iron with a fully polished interior, pre-seasoned with grapeseed oil, so it builds up seasoning the same way a skillet does and there’s no enamel coating to chip. The domed lid has drip channels on its underside that send condensation back down onto the food during a long braise. Expect some heft, since it weighs about 17.3 pounds with the lid. Smithey makes it in the US and backs it with a lifetime guarantee. Bare iron doesn’t love long simmers in tomato or wine, so save those braises for an enameled pot or keep them short.

Old cast iron is prized for its smooth, machined cooking surfaces, and Lancaster Cast Iron’s No. 8 Skillet brings that finish to a new pan. The cooking surface is polished smooth, then pre-seasoned with two layers of grapeseed oil at the company’s shop in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. The No. 8 measures 10.5 inches across the top, with a 9.25-inch cooking surface and 2-inch walls, and it weighs about 4 pounds. Polished iron starts out slick, and it gets slicker as layers of seasoning build up with every cook.

A saucier’s rounded bottom leaves no corners for a whisk or spatula to miss, which makes it the pan for custard and polenta and anything else that likes to scorch where the wall meets the floor. The Misen 3 QT Stainless Steel Saucier is 5-ply, with aluminum layers sandwiched inside stainless steel to spread heat across the base, and the walls are 3 millimeters thick. It measures about 9 inches across, comes with a lid, works on induction, and is oven-safe to 800°F. Misen backs it with a lifetime warranty against defects.

Kuhn Rikon’s 4th Burner Pot is tall and narrow, 5.5 inches across and holding 12 cups, so it fits on the small back burner while bigger pans take the front of the stove. That makes it handy for a couple of servings of pasta or a batch of blanched green beans. The glass lid has two built-in strainers and a pour spout, which lets you drain without hauling out a colander, and a removable basket inside handles steaming. Interior measurement marks save you a measuring cup, the silicone handles stay cool, and the stainless pot works on induction.

Microwave cooking goes better when steam is managed, and that’s the idea behind the Anyday 8-Piece Glass Round Dish Set. Each borosilicate glass dish gets a tempered glass lid with a silicone vent and gasket that let steam build and escape while the food cooks. Anyday says the stainless steel rim on each lid is microwave-safe as long as the dish sits at least an inch from the microwave’s walls. The set includes four dishes: two 4-cup sizes, one shallow and one deep, plus a 7-cup and an 8-cup. The bowls can go in the oven up to 500°F, so leftovers can get a crisp finish after they reheat.

Green tea scorches at a full boil, and pour-over coffee likes water a few degrees below it. The Fellow Corvo EKG Pro lets you dial in anywhere from 104 to 212 degrees Fahrenheit, then hold that temperature for 15 to 60 minutes so the second cup is as hot as the first. It also has an altitude setting, scheduling, and a pre-boil sanitize mode. The 0.9-liter body is 304 stainless steel. Fellow says the Wi-Fi only handles firmware updates, so you’ll still set the temperature on the kettle itself rather than from your phone.

Uneven grounds make uneven coffee, because the fine bits over-extract while the big chunks barely give up any flavor. The Fellow Ode Brew Grinder Gen 2 uses 64 mm stainless steel flat burrs, which cut a more uniform particle than the blade grinders most people start with. You get 11 settings split into 31 steps, a 100-gram capacity, and anti-static tech to keep grounds from clinging to the catch cup. Fellow built it for drip, pour-over, French press, and cold brew. It isn’t designed for espresso, so skip it for anyone pulling shots at home.

A coffee maker can only brew as well as its water temperature allows. The Moccamaster KBGV Select, handmade in the Netherlands, heats water quickly to brewing temperature with a copper boiling element, and the hot plate runs on its own separate element so it doesn’t cook the coffee sitting in the carafe. A switch on the brew basket adjusts the flow for a full 10-cup pot or a half batch, which keeps small batches from coming out thin. It carries the Specialty Coffee Association’s certification and a five-year warranty.

Most of the frustration of home espresso comes from dosing and grinding by feel. The Ninja Luxe Café Premier handles both: it has a conical burr grinder with 25 settings and a built-in scale that weighs the grounds for you, so each shot starts from a consistent dose. The Dual Froth System has four hands-free presets for steamed or frothed milk, and the machine also makes drip-style coffee and cold brew. It suits someone who wants café drinks without learning to tamp and time shots by eye.

Most countertop carbonators tell you to fizz plain water and add flavor afterward, because carbonating juice or wine tends to foam over. The Drinkmate OmniFizz gets around that with what the company calls its Fizz Infuser cap, which releases pressure gradually so you can carbonate cold drinks other than water. It runs on standard 60-liter CO2 cylinders, and Drinkmate sells it alone or in bundles with extra cylinders. Check the bundles before buying, since the kits with more cylinders were sometimes cheaper than the smaller ones in early November.

Matcha powder starts losing its color and flavor once it’s ground, which is why the Cuzen Matcha Maker grinds whole tea leaves on demand. Its hopper holds up to 20 grams of leaf, and the machine mills it, then mixes it with water in the cup using a magnetic whisk. You can pick a 1-, 1.5-, or 2-gram shot depending on how strong you like it, and there’s a grind-only mode for baking or lattes. The Starter Kit comes with 4-gram samples of three Cuzen leaf blends and a brush for cleaning the mill.

Pod-based cocktail machines lock you into one company’s drinks. The Barsys 360 uses whatever you put in it: six 750-milliliter canisters hold your own spirits, juices, and syrups, and a Bluetooth app tells the machine how much of each to pour through the spouts over the glass. It doesn’t shake or stir, so plan on finishing drinks the old-fashioned way. It also runs on USB-C power and weighs about 10 pounds empty, which makes it easier than you’d expect to move from the counter to a party table.

Nugget ice, the soft, chewable kind, is made by compressing ice flakes rather than freezing cubes in a tray. The GoveeLife Smart Nugget Ice Maker Pro does that on your counter, and Govee rates it for up to 60 pounds a day, with the first batch ready in about six minutes. A 4.9-liter side tank supplements the 2.2-liter main reservoir so you refill less often, and it has two self-cleaning cycles. You can also check on it or start it from the Govee app or by voice with Alexa or Google.

Centrifugal juicers spin produce against a fast blade, while slow juicers like the Hurom H310 Easy Clean press it with a turning screw at roughly 45 rotations per minute. Hurom’s version has a self-feeding hopper with a 50-millimeter chute that the company says fits whole apples, which cuts down on prep. Hurom backs the 150-watt motor with a 10-year warranty and covers the other parts for two years.

Boxed wine stays fresh longer than an open bottle, but the cardboard box is nobody’s idea of a centerpiece. The Boxxle Box Wine Dispenser is a stainless steel and ABS plastic housing for the bag inside a standard box. According to Boxxle, it lifts the bag so the spout sits above your glass and presses on the bag as it empties, so you can keep pouring until the last glass.

Fresh pasta dough needs to be rolled thin and evenly, and doing it with a rolling pin takes practice most people don’t have. The Marcato Atlas 150 is a hand-cranked roller with a 10-position thickness dial, so you can step the dough down a little at a time until it’s thin enough for lasagna sheets. The rollers are anodized aluminum, and the body is chrome-plated steel made in Italy. The version sold in the US includes fettuccine and spaghetti cutters, so you can go from sheet to noodles without buying attachments.

Most stand mixers drive a beater from above. The Ankarsrum Assistent Original flips that: its motor sits in the base and spins the 7-liter stainless steel bowl itself, while a dough hook or roller stays put. That design is why Ankarsrum says it can knead up to 5 kilograms of dough, a load that would stall a lot of tilt-head mixers. The Essential Package comes with a dough roller, dough knife, dough hook, spatula, and a proofing lid. Ankarsrum covers the base with a seven-year warranty, though accessories aren’t included.

Bread machines have a reputation for pale, unevenly baked tops. The Zojirushi Home Bakery Virtuoso Plus adds a heater in the lid to go with the usual one underneath, so the top of the loaf browns along with the sides. It bakes a 2-pound loaf and uses two kneading blades, which helps it work a full 2-pound batch of dough evenly.

Sourdough gets its crackly crust from steam trapped around the loaf early in the bake, which is why so many bakers use a Dutch oven. The Challenger Bread Pan rearranges that idea: you set the dough on a shallow cast-iron base and lower a tall domed lid over it, so you’re not dropping a floppy loaf into a deep, 500-degree pot. It weighs 20 pounds, is made in the USA, and is rated to 500 degrees Fahrenheit. Its 15.5-by-10.5-inch footprint fits oblong batards as well as round boules.

HexClad’s hybrid surface finally made the jump from frying pans to the oven. The HexClad Hybrid Baking Sheets use the same pattern of raised stainless steel hexagons with nonstick valleys in between, built over 2.5-millimeter tri-ply with an aluminum core. HexClad says the ceramic coating is free of PFAS and rates the sheets for oven temperatures up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re sold in two-packs in small and medium sizes, and the medium sheet measures 10 by 15 inches. HexClad says they’re dishwasher-safe but recommends washing them by hand.

Detroit-style pizza owes its crunchy, cheese-crisped edges to a deep rectangular pan that conducts heat fast. The LloydPans 10×14 Detroit-Style Pizza Pan is 2.5 inches deep and made from 14-gauge anodized aluminum in Spokane Valley, Washington. Its Pre-Seasoned Tuff-Kote finish means you can skip seasoning and use metal utensils on it, according to LloydPans. Spread the cheese all the way to the edges so it melts down the sides and fries against the metal.

Stretching pizza dough on a countertop usually ends with flour everywhere. The Gozney Pizza Prep Board has raised edges that keep the flour on the board and a catch tray at the back where you can sweep extra flour and reuse it. Its textured surface holds a thin, even coating of flour, which Gozney says works better than wood, steel, or marble at keeping dough from sticking and tearing on its way to the peel. A bench hook keeps it from sliding, and size markings go up to 16 inches. It’s 22 by 21.5 inches, so check counter space first.

Neapolitan pizza wants a stone near 850 degrees Fahrenheit, a temperature home ovens don’t reach. The Ooni Volt 2, successor to the Volt 12, gets there on a standard 120-volt outlet in about 20 minutes, according to Ooni. Inside is a 10-millimeter cordierite stone sized for 12-inch pizzas, and Ooni’s Pizza Intelligence system shifts power between the heating elements as you cook. Presets cover Neapolitan, thin and crispy, and pan pizza. At about 39 pounds, it’s heavy enough that you’ll want to give it a permanent spot.

Chef Nancy Silverton started with a quarter sheet pan when she helped Made In design this dish, then stretched it longer and wider. The Made In Porcelain Baking Slab is a 9-by-13-inch French porcelain dish fired three times in the Loire Valley, with a lower profile than a typical casserole so roasted vegetables and gratins get more browning. It’s oven-safe to 650 degrees Fahrenheit and microwave-safe, and it weighs 3.8 pounds. Made In’s care guide says it can go in the dishwasher, though the company’s FAQ recommends hand washing.

Nik Sharma’s newest book builds its 100 recipes around the science of flavor, explaining why each technique works. Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking came out from Chronicle Books in September 2026. It’s a good fit for the cook who keeps asking why a recipe calls for a specific step, and wants the answer along with dinner.

39 products that will improve your everyday life.

Brandt Ranj is an experienced writer for PopSci, covering topics such as science, technology, news, and gadget reviews.

Stan Horaczek is the executive gear editor at Popular Science. He oversees a team of gear-obsessed writers and editors dedicated to finding and featuring the newest, best, and most innovative gadgets on the market and beyond.

Popular Science started writing about technology more than 150 years ago. There was no such thing as “gadget writing” when we published our first issue in 1872, but if there was, our mission to demystify the world of innovation for everyday readers means we would have been all over it. Here in the present, PopSci is fully committed to helping readers navigate the increasingly intimidating array of devices on the market right now. Our writers and editors have combined decades of experience covering and reviewing consumer electronics. We each have our own obsessive specialties—from high-end audio to video games to cameras and beyond—but when we’re reviewing devices outside of our immediate wheelhouses, we do our best to seek out trustworthy voices and opinions to help guide people to the very best recommendations. We know we don’t know everything, but we’re excited to live through the analysis paralysis that internet shopping can spur so readers don’t have to. Find out more about our product evaluation process.
